en: Oṃ, salutation to the one whose supreme reality is the nature of the conscious self. Now begins the *Paramārthasāra* (The Essence of Ultimate Reality),
composed by the venerable and illustrious Abhinavaguptācārya, the most excellent teacher of the Great Maheśvara tradition.
Accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Yogarāja:
Victorious is the unborn Supreme Lord, who, though a mass of consciousness, has congealed into the form of the world; He is the masterful artist in the game of concealing His own nature. (1)

This Yoga, which has been composed by the Guru as a concise summary of the essence of the ultimate truth through reasoned methods, I shall provide a brief commentary upon, at the request of learned people. (2)

In this teaching of non-dual Śiva, considering that the completion of the scripture must first be preceded by the destruction of the flood of obstacles— consisting of doubt, fear, indolence, hesitation, and so forth, which arise from one's own volition when the predominance of the limited subjectivity of the body and such is maintained—

he first contemplates devotion to the Supreme Lord, which consists of an immersion into his own self as the deity— a mass of pure consciousness and bliss— and which encapsulates the essential meaning of the entire scripture by setting aside limited subjectivity.

I take refuge in You alone, Śambhu—the supreme, situated beyond, the one without beginning who dwells within the depths, yet is established manifoldly in the secret caverns; the abode of all, residing in everything moving and unmoving. // 1 //

I take refuge in You, Śambhu—the essence of the radiance of all subjects, whose very form is the deity of one’s own self, whose nature is the supreme good, and who consists of pure existence—as my protector for the sake of attaining the state of immersion in You.
The word "eva" (only) excludes any other connection, signifying: "I resort only to Śambhu, whose form is the deity of one's own self, and not to some separate deity wandering within Māyā.
Furthermore, what is He like? Supreme, full, overflowing with the powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, and possessing the unsurpassed essential nature.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "standing beyond the deep," he stands in his own essential nature within the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), which extends from that reality called "the Deep" (*gahana*)—namely, Māyā—up to the highest, full reality, ending with the *Śiva-vidyā* principle; he does not, however, fall away from that supreme, full essential nature even as it manifests through the various diversities of those respective states. As it has been said:
Even as it proceeds through the various states such as waking and so forth, which are non-different from it,
it never departs from its own essential nature as the perceiver.
Thus, in the Spandaśāstra:

"Beginningless" means ancient, because it is established from the very beginning as the subject (*pramātṛ*) by virtue of being the experiencer of all cognitions; "one" means without companion, because difference is untenable due to its manifestation as the unity of consciousness (*cidaikya*);
likewise, "pervaded," and so forth.

In this manner, though being of the nature of consciousness itself, he has entered within the "caves"—that is, the heart-caves—which are the forms of the Rudras and the individual souls (kṣetrajñas), appearing in many ways through various kinds of divisions by his own sovereignty.
Having manifested both the insentient and sentient natures for himself, he stands as the manifold subjects (pramātṛs) like an actor; such is the meaning.
For this very reason, it is called the "abode of all" (sarvālaya), meaning the place of rest for the entire universe consisting of subjects and objects, beginning with the Rudras and the kṣetrajñas.

All this, it is said, resides within the Perfect Subject (*pūrṇapramātṛ*); depending on the pair of subject and object, it appears as if emergent through differentiation and is designated by various forms. Otherwise, being distinct from its manifestation, it would have no existence at all—how then could there be this universe? Such is the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the pronoun "all" (*sarva*).
He states that the true nature of the Blessed One is not transcended by this much alone, saying: "Abiding in all that is moving and unmoving.

Since you abide as the very form of this entire universe, which consists of both the insentient and the sentient, and since you are the creator of all, O All-pervading Lord, therefore you yourself are indeed this entire world.

For, according to this principle, it is impossible for anything else that is distinct [from the Self] and not manifesting itself to be an effect. Thus, as it is said: "The enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment"; the Blessed Lord himself shines forth in such and such ways.

I take refuge in you, O Lord Śambhu, who are of such a nature—supreme, the essential form of one's own self as deity for all, whose core is the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*), yet who has assumed manifold forms; who, though possessing the nature of the light of supreme non-duality and unbroken self-sovereignty, nevertheless subordinates the artificial egoity of the body and so forth. I take refuge in you alone, my own self, who are of such a nature—the very essence of the wonder of supreme I-consciousness.
"I enter into [it]"—this much is the meaning.

By this introductory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*), the Guru, teaching the state that consists of the entry into one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*) as the supreme object of attainment, has already introduced the subject matter of the entire treatise according to what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as will be explained hereafter. Having thus established the intent of the work—the non-dual nature of reality—by means of praise, the author now states the introduction of the scripture, including its connection (*saṃbandha*), subject matter (*abhidheya*), and so forth, in two Āryā verses.
Having wandered through the wheel of suffering beginning with dwelling in the womb and ending with death, the disciple questioned the Blessed One, the support, regarding the ultimate truth. // 2 //
Abhinavagupta explains that essence, as spoken by the Guru through the *Ādhārakārikās*, by means of the perspective of the Śiva-scripture. 3.

A certain person, having developed detachment through the grace of the Blessed One and with a mind turned away from cyclic existence, thinking "I am to be instructed by my guru," properly propitiated the true guru, the blessed sage named Śeṣa, who is the foundation, and questioned him regarding the nature of the instruction on the ultimate reality.
Then, through the process of examining the ripening of that disciple's fitness, [the guru], perceiving that the disciple’s internal organ had been purified, [proceeded].

That Anantanātha, who was fully conversant with the instructions of all the scriptures, taught this disciple— according to the doctrine of Sāṃkhya as set forth in his work titled *Paramārthasāra*, also known by the alternative name *Ādhārakārikā*— that the attainment of the Supreme Brahman results from the knowledge of the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

That very same instruction regarding Brahman, when presented from the perspective of one's own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) which is the nature of supreme non-duality, is established as being endowed with logical reasoning.

Thinking that [this teaching] exists for the sake of favoring all people, the Guru—being "Gupta," meaning secret, hidden, and endowed with esoteric secrets (*sarahasya*)—through the logic of the supreme non-dual Śaiva system, by means of a fresh and extraordinary expansion of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*), sets forth that essence which is the very core of that instruction on the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This essence, like butter extracted from curd, is what is to be adopted; and being intent on favoring others, he now imparts it.
Thus, the connection, the subject matter, the title, and the purpose have been established; they will not be elaborated upon here again for fear of making this treatise too voluminous.
As to what kind of disciple he is, he says: "concerning the dwelling in the womb.
[The stages of life] arise, exist, grow, transform, decline, and perish, beginning with the dwelling in the womb.

Wandering—that is, revolving—upon that wheel which, through its diversity of various states, is joined with the rim of the six transformations of existence; which consists of the nature of suffering ending only in death; and which, by its nature of saṃsāra consisting of manifestation and disappearance, is like a wheel:

by this [description], his prior nature of remembering former births and the manifestation of awakening are illuminated; otherwise, how could there be such curiosity regarding inquiry, characterized by the attainment of the ultimate goal?
And thus, he who has attained detachment, whose heart has been pierced by the power of the Supreme Lord’s grace, in whom right knowledge has arisen, and who,

having become a fit vessel for instruction, encounters a suitable Guru who embodies the form of the Supreme Lord and desires the supreme non-dual knowledge— he alone shall be a recipient of the Guru’s instruction.
And this very point has been stated elsewhere:
"O Goddess, by the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), one is led toward a true guru.
This will also be explained here later on. // 3 //

Now, having established the introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) by means of the process of emanation (*samutpattikrama*), the author introduces the treatise, demonstrating through the four cosmic eggs (*aṇḍacatuṣṭaya*) that in this world—a variegated painting of universal diversity—it is solely the unsurpassed sovereignty of the Supreme Lord that is the cause of the agency of joining and disjoining; thus, he shows that the universe is nothing but the unfolding of His power:
"By the weight of the majesty of His own power, He [divides] these four cosmic eggs according to their divisions."
Power (śakti), illusion (māyā), primordial nature (prakṛti), and earth (pṛthvī) were brought forth by the Lord.

By the Lord Maheśvara, who is independent and the Blessed One consisting of a single mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), this fourfold egg (*aṇḍacatuṣṭaya*) has been manifested—meaning revealed or employed as the agent of manifestation—as a solid mass of substance in the form of a sheath that covers the universe. As it is said:
"A solid mass of substance is called an egg.
It has been brought forth by his power of becoming.
He asks "Why? and replies: "Because of the weight of the majesty of His own power.

"His own" (*nija*) means belonging to Himself; that which is the unique accumulation of powers, beginning with Will (*icchā*), its "majesty" (*vaibhava*) is its manifold expansion, and the "weight" (*bhara*) is its intense surge.
Indeed, for the Blessed One, the very unfolding of the expansion of His own power is the creation of the universe.
As it is stated in the Śrī-Sarvamaṅgalā-śāstra:
"Power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimān)—these two are said to be the fundamental categories.
All this world is his powers, while the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of power."
Thus [it is asked]: what is the enumeration of the fourfold egg (*aṇḍa*)? He says: "Power (*śakti*), Māyā, Nature (*prakṛti*), and Earth.

That supreme power of the Lord, which consists of the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) whose nature is the concealment of one's own true form, and which takes the form of the activity of negation, is called the "egg of power" (*śaktyaṇḍa*) because it acts as a veil and a cause of bondage for the universe—which, though its essence is the wonder of the supreme I-consciousness, appears in the form of subjects and objects.

This power is designated by this term because it exists in the form of a sheath (*kośa*), having internally and completely encompassed the three eggs (*aṇḍa*) to be described later, which extend as far as the principles (*tattva*) of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā.
Within this egg, Sadāśiva and Īśvara themselves are the presiding lords.

Furthermore, that which consists of the nature of the three impurities (mala), is composed of delusion (moha), and—due to its exclusive inclination toward differentiation—constitutes the bondage for all subjects (pramātṛs) down to the level of the *puruṣa-tattva*, is called the Egg (aṇḍa) named Māyā.
And it stands encompassing within itself, on all sides, the two Eggs to be described later.
The Lord of this Egg is the Rudra known as Gahana.

Likewise, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, having transformed itself into the form of effects and instruments, becomes the object of enjoyment for the bound subjects (*paśu-pramātṛs*). Being the cause of bondage through the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it is called the "egg" (*aṇḍa*) known as *prakṛti*. Within that too, the Lord Viṣṇu, possessed of great majesty, presides over the egg as its sovereign, characterized by differentiation. Similarly, the earth, acting as a gross sheath in the form of successive enclosures for all subjects from humans down to stationary beings, is called the "earth-egg" (*pṛthvy-aṇḍa*) because it binds them.
Even therein, among the fourteenfold creation of beings, the Lord Brahmā is the sovereign of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍādhipa*) by virtue of his preeminence.
Thus, this fourfold cosmic egg, which is the manifestation of the Supreme Lord, shines forth as it has been revealed by the Blessed One in this manner. // 4 //

Having thus established these four pillars, he now states a verse to define the nature of the universe by focusing on the presentation of the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed within this very context:
"Within that [universe], there exists this manifold continuity of bodies, instruments, and worlds;
and the enjoyer therein is the embodied soul, who is none other than Śiva himself having assumed the state of a bound creature (paśu). (Kārikā 5)
Within those four eggs well-known from the scriptures, this entire universe exists in their midst.
To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "Variegated.

The bodies—meaning forms—consisting of various arrangements of faces, hands, feet, and so forth, which are divided by the distinctions between Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas), exist as wonders in the form of specific configurations.
Likewise, the instruments such as the eyes and so forth differ from one another and possess degrees of excellence.

For instance, the instruments of subjects such as Rudra are unsurpassed and endowed with a multitude of qualities such as omniscience; it is said that by means of these, all this [universe] is known and accomplished simultaneously in a single moment.

However, for the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls), these very same instruments are constrained by the power of destiny (*niyati*) of the Supreme Lord; they are capable only of producing knowledge of limited objects such as jars and the like, and everything is not known by them.

Nor is it produced [by them]. In that regard, too, there is a preeminent power of the yogins' instruments, by which, through transcending the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), even that which is distant, obstructed, or remote is discerned with their own instruments, and the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in other subjects are known.
And thus, even among animals, although their faculties are contracted by the power of destiny, there exists a superiority even over humans.
For example: cows see their own homes even when obstructed; horses perceive the path even at night;
vultures behold a carcass even at a distance of a hundred *yojanas*; and birds, down to the flies and mosquitoes, move through the sky.
Reptiles are seen to travel along paths on their bellies and hear sounds with their eyes; camels hear from a great distance, and dogs draw out a snake from its hole by means of their breath alone.
In this way, the diversity of the instruments [of perception] is to be inferred in all cases.
Likewise, the worlds, as established by scripture, possess extraordinary configurations in the form of circles, triangles, squares, half-moons, and parasols.

Thus, this universe (*viśva*) is that in which there exists such a continuum of these bodies, instruments, and worlds—a continuous flow of uninterrupted bondage—characterized by various extraordinary and marvelous natures.
And since there must be an enjoyer for such a universe whose nature consists of objects of enjoyment, he says: "And the enjoyer therein is the embodied soul."

The body, which is the locus of experience, exists for that individual soul (*aṇu*) who is afflicted by the three impurities (*malatraya*); he is the "embodied one" (*dehī*), whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and so forth. In this world composed of pleasure, pain, and the like, he is the "enjoyer" (*bhoktā*), the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and is called the "subject as a bound soul" (*paśupramātā*).

Now, one might object: from the perspective of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), not even the slightest atom possesses any duality; how then can there exist such a wretched thing as an "embodied one" distinct from that? As it has been said:
"Even a single portion of Brahman does not transcend its possession of all forms and is beyond conceptualization.
Thus,
even within each individual principle (*tattva*), there exists the nature of all thirty-six principles.

And according to this principle, the Supreme Lord alone—the Great Light whose very nature is consciousness, endowed with His own power—is the subject (*pramātā*), appearing entirely non-different from all things.
Therefore, even if one were to assume the existence of an embodied being (*dehin*) distinct from Him, its reality could not be established because it would be impossible for such a thing to manifest;
for if it does manifest, then within that Supreme Brahman-Self, it must be the one subject who is non-different from the Light itself. Thus, once again...

Establishing the entire argument that this differentiation—characterized by the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer—is [ultimately] for the sake of what, he says: "Śiva himself has assumed the state of the bound soul (paśu).
This Lord Śiva, who was just described as a single mass of consciousness and bliss, whose very nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya), [is he].
That very [Self], while remaining in its true nature yet concealing it through its own will, assumes—like an actor—the role of the embodied subject;

and because it is to be protected (*pālya*) and because it is a bound soul (*paśu*), characterized by the state of being a beast (*paśutva*), it is called the "embodied enjoyer" (*dehī*) with respect to this object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) composed of pleasure, pain, and so forth, which it has fashioned for itself. However, there is no collection of objects whatsoever that exists apart from Śiva.

And it is this very Lord Śiva who, by his absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), brings forth as if in play the dyad of subject and object—characterized as enjoyer and enjoyed—which is the basis for this predominance of duality.

Therefore, this alone is the unsurpassed sovereignty of the Supreme Lord: that even while having attained the state of a bound soul (*paśu*) characterized by the nature of enjoyer and enjoyed through the abandonment of His full essential nature, He remains within Himself as the experiencer of all subjects.
He is indeed Śiva, the single solid mass of throbbing consciousness and bliss. // 5 //

Even so, if that single conscious nature (*citsvabhāva*)—the subject—is manifold due to the diversity of subjects and objects such as *māyā* and the rest, how can it be designated as one despite being contradictory? If it is one, why does it have manifold forms? Because of the contradiction, like shadow and light, there arises the superimposition of contradictory attributes; for a single entity cannot simultaneously be of manifold forms. As it has been said:
"This very thing is the distinction and the cause of distinction among entities, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties or a difference in their causes.
Thus, demonstrating a worldly example here, he establishes the objection regarding the subject of the analogy:
"Just as a pure crystal assumes the form of various colors..."
Just as [the reflection] takes on the form of gods, humans, animals, or trees, so too does the Lord.

Just as even a single crystal gem, by assuming within itself the various diversities produced by a thousand different adjuncts such as lac-dye, indigo, and so forth, becomes variegated in that way, yet its status as a crystal is not lost thereby; indeed, it is precisely this that constitutes the "gem-nature" of the crystal gem— that despite being colored by those various particularities, there is for everyone at all times an uncontradicted cognition that "this is a crystal gem."

It is merely said that "these lac-dyes and so forth shine here," but the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as lac does not qualify the gem as a cloth does, such that there would be a loss of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, this very state of being stainless belongs to the gem: that it assumes forms which are the nature of the adjuncts, yet manifests itself through its own essential nature.

In exactly the same way, this Lord (*Īśvara*), who is independent, a single mass of consciousness, and though one, [reflects] within the clear mirror of His own Self all beings ending with gods, humans, animals, birds, and immovable things.

Maintaining— as if through non-difference from its own self— the state of being the form of particular objects such as the *rudra*, the *kṣetrajña*, and so forth, both those created by itself and those [created] by others, as well as the variety of colors like a crystal gem, and because it has transcended even that, it reflects upon its own self as "I" alone— a single self that, though possessing manifold forms, is augmented by an indivisible wonder.

Thus, for this Great Lord who is one's own Self, there exists no distinct space or time whatsoever that could serve as a basis for attributing defects such as the coexistence of contradictory attributes.

Even the variegated cognition characterized by direct perception—which is divided into various distinctions—is accepted by others as being indeed one. Just as in a variegated cognition, the blue and other colors are adjuncts of the cognition itself and do not exist apart from it.
For one who discriminates with respect to that object which is impossible to perceive falls [into error].
Thus it is stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*.

But how could these two— space and time— which are considered to be the factors that differentiate the Knower who is complete in every respect, whose sole body is consciousness, and who is autonomous,
and which exist as the manifestors of His manifold forms and manifold actions— belong to that very Blessed One?
[The two] would be mutually exclusive.

If indeed space and time were at any point established as distinct from consciousness, then an imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) caused by that [distinction] might arise, and in that case, such a possibility would exist.

However, since the existence of those two is established solely through the manifestation of consciousness, the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), who is of a single nature despite possessing manifold aspects, is established as having consciousness as his very form; furthermore, regarding the attribute of difference, there is no imposition of contradictory attributes.
It is indeed difficult to extract. // 6 //

Now, if it is argued that the cognizer, whose true nature is consciousness alone, having assumed the state of body, organs, and world, has thereby attained multiplicity—then, upon the destruction of the body and so forth, he himself would be destroyed; and upon their production, he himself would be produced at that time.

In this way, for every individual cognizer, he himself is differentiated through the sixfold modifications of existence, such as being born and existing, according to the variety of karma consisting of merit and demerit.
If it is argued that the Blessed One experiences enjoyments such as heaven and hell, how can it be said that he is Śiva in his very own nature?
This point is also established by means of an illustration:
"Just as the reflection of the moon moves when [the water] moves, and comes to rest when [the water] is still."
In the same way, this Great Lord, the Self, [is the cause] within the aggregate of bodies, instruments, and worlds. // 7 //
Just as when a current of water flows, the orb of the moon— the lunar body which, by its actual nature, remains motionless while situated in the sky—

appears to move and travel even though it has fallen within that flowing water; and likewise, at that very same moment, when another body of water becomes still, that very same lunar orb appears to come to rest— thus is this imagined in both ways by all cognizing subjects.
Furthermore, it would not be so in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Nor do the place and time located in the water act as differentiators for the nature of the moon situated in the sky;
rather, it is merely the water itself that appears in such a way, and yet [there are qualities] such as the movement or lack of movement belonging to the lunar disc reflected therein.
The mere fact that "difference" is conventionally expressed does not cause any impairment to the true nature of the moon, whether it is reflected in the waters of the Gaṅgā or fallen into mud.

In the same way, this Self, whose intrinsic nature is consciousness, is merely a conventional expression for those deluded by *māyā*—who think it has perished or arisen when the aggregate of the body, organs, and worlds created by itself has perished or arisen; it is like the moon reflected in water.
Furthermore, [the question arises] whether one's own self is born or dies;
it has been stated exactly thus in the Gītā:
"It is never born nor does it ever die; nor, having come to be, will it ever cease to be."
Unborn, eternal, ever-lasting, and ancient, this [Self] is not slain when the body is slain.

Thus, this Self is the Great Lord (*maheśāna*), autonomous, whose essential nature is the reflective awareness of its own totality. While manifesting as the experiencer of all subjects, it remains in its very own nature whether there is the dissolution or the arising of various states. And this is precisely the power of the Great Lordship of the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*)—that which performs the impossible: even while experiencing enjoyments such as heaven and hell through the state of being a bound subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*), it remains the very nature of consciousness by virtue of being the experiencer of everything.
On the contrary, if this state of being a beast— consisting of merit, demerit, heaven, hell, hunger, thirst, and so forth— which is determined to be bondage,
were illuminated and grasped by the Blessed One through the light of his own Self, then [one would realize] that which was previously described within one's own Self.
Otherwise, it would possess no intrinsic nature at all; how then could it be said that this very Maheśvara brings about the destruction of his own essential nature?

In every respect, only a created entity—such as the body and so forth—can be produced or withdrawn; however, production and destruction can never occur within the eternal Lord, who is pure consciousness.

Therefore, the Self is indeed one, yet possessing a manifold nature by way of being the grasped and the grasper; furthermore, as the experiencer of all and through the unity of everything, it manifests—thus there is no injury whatsoever to the doctrine of non-duality.

Thus, if it has been established through both reasoning and scripture that this Self of all is indeed the very nature of the universal manifestation (*viśvaprapañca*), whose ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra-paramārtha*), and who is the illumination of everything because consciousness permeates everywhere— then why is it not perceived as one's own Self even in a clod of earth and the like, since there is no difference [between them]? Or, if it were so accepted, this manifest distinction between the insentient and the sentient would not be tenable, nor would worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*).
To the question, "How can it be that [the Self] has both an insentient and a sentient form? he says:

Just as Rāhu, though invisible, becomes manifest when situated within the lunar orb, so too this Self, although omnipresent, becomes manifest by taking on objects within the mirror of the intellect (dhī). (8)

Just as Rāhu, though wandering everywhere in the space of the sky, is not perceived, yet at the time of an eclipse he is recognized as "this is Rāhu" when he appears stationed upon the form of the moon— otherwise, even while situated in the stellar sphere, he is as if non-existent— so too here, although this Self exists as the innermost of all, it is not perceived by anyone in that way, because its nature consists solely of self-experience and thus it is not directly visible [as an object].

Furthermore, when the subjects consisting of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) perceive objects such as sound through the mirror of the intellect (buddhi-darpaṇa)— that is, at the time of establishing the status of the grasped—
the Self becomes the object of the cognition "I hear" and so forth by way of assuming those objects. At that time,

although it exists even in a clod of earth and the like by virtue of being the nature of the grasper, its own self shines forth there in a manifest form, and for everyone, it is of the singular nature of one's own direct experience.
Just as Rāhu, because he consists of absolute darkness, is perceived in the sky as if non-existent even though he is present,

so too this Lord, by means of his power of māyā, makes certain portions of the objective world— which, though identical with his own self, are of the nature of the *puryaṣṭaka*— into subjects of cognition (*vedaka*) when they are consecrated by the essence of the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*),

while making others into objects of cognition (*vedya*). It is in relation to this that the conventional usage of duality, consisting of the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, becomes well-established and logically tenable.

Therefore, because a clod of earth and the like are objects of cognition (*vedya*), they are insentient (*jaḍa*); and because the subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* is the cognizer (*vedaka*), it is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*).
However, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārtha*) in relation to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the distinction between the insentient and the non-insentient does not exist. // 8 //

Now, if it is the case that the self flashes forth without distinction within the intellect of all cognizers, then why would they all not be knowers of their own self? Or, let them not be possessors of that knowledge, for there is no difference [in the nature of the self].

Yet, even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), some are seen to be liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) through the knowledge of their own self, endowed with omniscience and omnipotence;

others are seen to be merely fit for the knowledge of their own self and desirous of ascending [the path]; while still others, being devoid of the knowledge of their own self, remain bound by the continuous fetters of auspicious and inauspicious karma caused by merit and demerit.

"How can it be consistent that [the descent of power] belongs only to those in saṃsāra?"— having thus established everything internally, he demonstrates that the descent of power from the Supreme Lord is unshackled:
"Just as a face shines forth in a mirror free from impurity, so too is this."
In the principle of consciousness, purified by the descent of Śiva’s power, that which consists of light shines forth.

Just as a face shines in a mirror free from impurity, endowed with its full range of qualities such as form and so forth without distinction— there is no place that a mirror whose stains have been removed does not embrace— yet in a soiled mirror, even a face that possesses no inferiority appears distorted due to its own turbidity.
Nor is one who is impure capable of appropriating His qualities;

on the contrary, a person with his face turned toward Him, seeing his own face as something quite different—possessed of darkness and other such defects—bears shame within himself, thinking, "My face is deformed.
In the very same way, regarding Śiva, there is His power called *anugraha* (grace); its "fall" (*pāta*) is the expansion of its own rays. By that [power],...

When the mirror of intuition has been cleansed—rendered clear through the exhaustion of the latent impressions of the impurities of finitude (*āṇava*), cosmic illusion (*māyīya*), and action (*kārmika*)—the light, that is, the radiance, whose nature is luminosity (*bhārūpa*), shines forth for certain cognizing subjects in their final birth. This self-nature manifests in its entirety, including all its attributes such as omniscience;
by means of this manifestation of the true nature of their own self, even while remaining in the midst of transmigratory existence, they are as if liberated and possess extraordinary excellence.

In some individuals, when the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) is completely veiled by the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*—which are the powers of the Supreme Lord’s power of concealment—the Self, though consisting of light, appears as if non-apparent due to that defilement; for this reason, they are called *paśu*s (bound souls) who wander in saṃsāra.
Others, however, being subjects (*pramātṛ*) through the conjunction of both powers [of grace and concealment], are called those "desirous of ascending" (*ārurukṣavaḥ*).
In this way, the diversity of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—distinguished by degrees such as intense, mild, or very mild—is to be inferred everywhere.

Here, no ritual act whatsoever—such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), or anything else arising from the power of necessity (*niyatiśakti*) which falls within the sphere of *māyā*—can be the cause of the soul’s liberation; for since that soul has transcended *māyā*, [such acts] would serve only to accomplish objects characterized by duality.
It is not logically tenable [to claim otherwise], as it has been sung:
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice [is this attained].
Therefore, in this matter, for those of noble intellect, the sole cause is the unconditioned grace of the Supreme Lord. As it has been said:
When the portion of the Lord's descent of power (śaktipāta) is manifested,
the intellect— permeated by the aspect of His absolute freedom— requires nothing at all.

Thus [it is said]. For individual subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*), however, the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) belonging to the Supreme Lord is precisely the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). By means of this, because their own true nature does not manifest, they are intent upon auspicious and inauspicious karma and partake in the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
thus they transmigrate again and again in this world.

Therefore, although the self is common to all subjects, it consists of both manifestation and non-manifestation; therein lie two powers alone—grace (*anugraha*) and concealment—which are the causes for the distinction between liberation and bondage. As it has been said:
An unimpeded power of the one possessing infinite power binds the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with the nets of the snares of worldly existence;
yet another [power], having cut away all the qualities (guṇas) with the sword of knowledge, brings the person face-to-face with liberation.
Thus [ends the ninth].

Having thus established that all this is consistent with scripture, experience, and reasoning, [the author] now speaks in two verses concerning the nature of Paramaśiva, the primary cause of all causes, upon which the universe— consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) arising through the sequence of emanation and existing within the previously described fourfold egg (*aṇḍa*) beginning with Śakti— rests as it shines forth.
It is the form of light, complete through resting within its own self as great bliss;
it is filled with the instruments of will and consciousness, and is replete with infinite powers.
In that Supreme Reality— which is devoid of all conceptual construction, pure, peaceful, and free from both dissolution and emergence—
the universe consisting of thirty-six principles shines forth.

That is to say: in that very supreme, perfect Śiva-tattva, the entire universe—beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, as will be described hereafter—is revealed while resting within it; it is logically established that [the universe] shines forth as non-different from that [Śiva-tattva].

Now, one might object: "That is called a *tattva* (reality/principle) wherein everything, such as the body (*tanu*) and so forth, is extended (*tanyate*); or else, because of its extension (*tananāt*), it is the state (*bhāva*) of that [extension] until the dissolution (*pralaya*)."
Or even if it is called "reality" (*tattva*), how could this designation of reality apply to the Lord Paramaśiva, whose nature is consciousness, since such a term would imply insentience?

It is said that the designation "reality" is applied to him only insofar as he is expressed by whatever words are used for the sake of those to be instructed; it does not exist there in an ultimate sense.
What, then, is that supreme reality?
"Luminosity" (*bhās*) means light; its nature is form, which signifies that its body is great illumination.
Likewise, it is "perfectly full," meaning free from all desire.
Since even insentient things such as crystal, gems, and mirrors are free from desire, he says "great bliss through resting in one's own self" to distinguish it from them.

"Great bliss" (*mahānānanda*) refers to one for whom there is supreme satisfaction (*parā nirvṛtiḥ*) arising from resting in the essence of the wonder of indivisible I-consciousness within one's own nature.
Thus, because its core is the radiance that brings about supreme delight, it is shown to be distinct from inert things such as crystal, which are merely objects of illumination.
For this very reason, he says: "filled with the instruments of the consciousness of will."

It is indeed of the very nature of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*); it is not, however, devoid of power or nearly insentient like the Brahman of those who propound a quiescent [Brahman].
Furthermore, it is "filled with infinite powers.
Infinite means innumerable; the powers consisting of names and forms, such as pots, cloths, and so forth, are the offshoots of the powers of will, knowledge, and action.

The powers beginning with Brāhmī arise from the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi); by them [the universe] is completely filled and pervaded on all sides. Thus, they emerge from that very source and dissolve back into it. In this way, the Lord’s sovereignty, whose nature is the Supreme Speech (parāvāk), has been described.

Now, one might object: "If the supreme reality is of the nature of speech (*vāgrūpa*), then it must be conceptual because it is permeated by sound; how can there be any possibility of conceptualization within the essence of pure luminosity? With this intention, [the author] says: "devoid of all conceptual constructions" (*sarvavikalpavihīnam*).
This wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā-camatkāra*) within the supreme subject, though of the nature of speech, is free from conceptualization.

For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), determines a jar by excluding what is not a jar, while implying a duality consisting of the forms of "jar" and "non-jar."

Furthermore, for Light— which has as its essence the wonder of supreme subjectivity (parāhaṃtā)— there exists no opposite that is non-luminous or distinct from Light, through the exclusion of which Light might assume a conceptualized form.
For if an object to be excluded, being non-luminous by nature, were to appear within the body of Light, then it would do so by way of being identical with it,
through the very nature of its perception.

By this principle, how could an object that has attained the nature of luminosity (*prakāśasvabhāvatā*) be its own delimiter, such that it would bring about the state of conceptualization (*vikalparūpatā*) therein? Furthermore, if it does not manifest as an opposite, how could it even be possible to determine that a non-manifesting entity exists here as an opposite form? This [objection] would be trivial. For the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*) is devoid of all conceptualizations consisting of exclusion (*vyavacchedātmakaiḥ vikalpaiḥ*) and possesses an undelimited nature (*aparicchinnasvabhāva*).

For this very reason, he says "pure," meaning stainless, because of the absence of the impurity consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Likewise, it is "quiescent" because of the absence of agitation arising from the grasped and the grasper; thus, by virtue of the equilibrium of power (*śakti-sāmarasya*), it abides in its own essential nature, and is not like a mere fragment of stone.
Furthermore, it is "devoid of dissolution and arising";
for, having established that this Self is "shining forth once and for all," it is indeed eternal.

Therefore, since time—consisting of past, future, and present—does not operate there, it is precisely from that [Supreme Reality] that the manifestation of time arises; thus, when the Supreme Principle is accepted as being devoid of origination and destruction, it would be demonstrated that the "universality" of the universe is logically established. // 11 //

Now, as for what has been established—that the world appears within such a supreme reality (paratattva)—how can this be so? For, in relation to the supreme reality, nothing at all would be capable of appearing as distinct from it. If the world appears as separate from that, then the doctrine of non-duality (advayavāda) is undermined; if, on the other hand, the world shines forth as non-distinct, how can one even speak of it [as appearing]? To demonstrate the nature of that reality as both distinct and non-distinct by means of an illustration, he says the following to support this point:
"Just as in the reflection of a mirror, a variegated array of cities, villages, and so forth, though diverse, is indivisible..."
And it shines forth through mutual distinction, even as from a mirror.

Through the supremely pure and ultimate realization of Bhairava, this world— which, though devoid of division, appears as if divided from one another and even from that [realization] itself— shines forth.

Just as within the interior of a stainless mirror, everything—cities, villages, towns, walls, watchtowers, ground, rivers, streams, fires, trees, mountains, animals, birds, women, men, and so forth—appears as a variegated reflection; though it shines with its own specific characteristics in various forms, it remains undivided from the mirror.
While appearing as non-different from it, it presents its internal form precisely through that non-difference, yet it shines even as it appears there by way of distinction alone.

And "mutually" means that by virtue of their own specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*), the cloth is distinct from the jar and the jar is distinct from the cloth; thus they manifest as differentiated.

For it is indeed the entities contained within that mirror which are perceived as separate, yet nothing at all is apprehended apart from that mirror. Rather, even while existing in a state of identity with the mirror, the world is perceived as being distinct on all sides.
Even so, one might argue that the mirror would then be hidden by the reflection of the jar and other objects; to this he says, "And even from the mirror," meaning no.

Not only do entities appear as distinct when they have entered within the mirror, but they appear as distinct even from the mirror itself, because the mirror, although composed of those various reflections, remains in its essential nature transcending those reflections.
It shines forth, yet it does not become identical with that [reflection], nor is it perceived as "not being a mirror.
Furthermore, even when everyone perceives various reflections therein, the cognition "this is a mirror" remains uncontradicted.
Nor do objects such as jars qualify the mirror in such a way that its own nature would be lost, leading to such designations as "this is a jar-mirror" or "this is a cloth-mirror."
Whether the difference is produced by place or by time, it does not result in the destruction of the intrinsic nature [of the mirror].

Therefore, while being capable of receiving various reflections, the mirror remains a mirror within itself; thus, there is no impairment whatsoever to the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*). Now, it might be argued: "The notion that 'there is an elephant in the mirror' is an error (*bhrānti*); however, no such thing exists in the mirror at all, because it lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) in its true nature, and this conviction arises solely through delusion."
Thus,
by this much of the theory of reflection (pratibimbavāda), the illustrative example is established for now;
the true nature of error, however, will be examined immediately hereafter.

In the same way, by means of the analogy of reflections in a mirror, city, and so forth, from the light of the supremely pure and ultimate Bhairava-consciousness— which is intensely free from temporal limitations and overflowing with full-blown bliss— the entire universe, though devoid of division and undivided from that light like a reflection in a mirror, appears as if divided from one another in relation to the subject and object.

"And it manifests as manifold form even from that"— meaning that because it appears as if emerged even from consciousness (*bodha*), since consciousness itself manifests in the form of those [objects], it therefore manifests as transcending them, just as a mirror [transcends] its reflections. In this way, the Light (*prakāśa*), which is capable of receiving the reflections of all objective existents, manifests in its own essential nature as the experiencer of everything, transcending all objective existents.
Even when objects are present, the distinctions of place, time, and form manifest here merely like reflections in a mirror, yet they do not break apart its own nature.
For this very reason, although consciousness possesses both a single and manifold nature, it remains one alone, just like the variegated cognition accepted by the Buddhists.

However, there is this much distinction between the light of the mirror and the light of Consciousness (cit) which possesses wonder: that in the mirror, there is only the accompaniment of sheer transparency.

An external object such as a city, which is conceived as a reflection, appears as something distinct; it does not, however, manifest as something created by [the mirror] itself. Therefore, the determination that "this is an elephant in the mirror" would be an error. Light (prakāśa), on the other hand, whose essence is its own wonder, manifests the entire universe—using its own consciousness as the material cause—by freely perceiving it non-differently upon the wall of its own self through its own will.

The Lord’s state of being a creator is nothing other than the manifestation of the universe; thus, this very act of self-awareness (*parāmarśa*) is the primary form of Light that distinguishes it from inert reflections such as those in a mirror.
This very point was stated by the author in the *Vivṛtivimarśinī*:
"Just as the entire world with its diverse arrangements shines within a mirror, so does everything shine here within the Self."
Furthermore, consciousness perceives the universe through the method of its own essential self-reflection; a mirror, however, does not do so.

Thus, with respect to the Supreme Lord, there is no delusion of duality whatsoever in the multitude of entities created from His own limbs; however, with respect to the subject under the influence of *māyā*, this appearance of duality is a delusion consisting of the non-recognition (*akhyāti*) of fullness. This means that the nature of the Full, which is non-dual, is not manifested or made known;
rather than the Full appearing, the incomplete dual form appears, such that only duality is perceived.
Therefore, this theory of the reflected image is irreproachable. // 13 //

Thus, having first established the nature of the supreme reality (paratattva) and having set forth the existence of the universe— consisting of thirty-six principles— as non-different from the Light (prakāśa), he again explains the essential nature of each principle according to the order of its emergence through these verses: [the state of the principles] consisting of Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā.
It manifests the five powers through their differentiated states. // 14 //

This Supreme Śiva, whose nature has just been explained through the determination of the supreme reality (paratattva), possesses five powers— known as consciousness (cit), bliss (nirvṛti), will (icchā), knowledge (jñāna), and action (kriyā)— which constitute his own essential form and serve as the cause for the multitude of infinite powers.
It is precisely by distinguishing these five powers from one another, through the exclusion of what they are not, that this state of reality (tattvadaśā) is delimited by the number five.
"It illuminates" means that it makes manifest by way of its own specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*).
To the question "Of what kind is she?", he says "Śiva," and so forth.
She is described as such because her nature (*bhāva*) consists of Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva. Likewise, she is described as such because her primordial matter (*prakṛti*) consists of Īśvara and Vidya.
Here, the essential nature of each principle (*tattva*) is demonstrated.

For instance, that consciousness which exists within all subjects—consisting of the wonder of the fullness of the "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), transcending all principles, and whose body is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*)—is precisely the Śiva-principle.
In this context, the determination of the principles is made with a view toward those who are to be instructed.

Of that very Blessed One, whose nature is consciousness (*cit*), who reflects "I become the universe" in the form of bliss (*ānanda*), there is this state of power (*śaktyavasthā*): it is consciousness itself, consisting of the essential nature of all things, which, taking the form of a slight swelling, is the seed-ground of all existents. Although this very [consciousness] possesses the forms of both the thin and the full through the metaphorical application of the emission and withdrawal of the universe, it is proclaimed as one alone in all the systems of secret doctrine.

Furthermore, in this very ground which is the seed of the universal emergence, known as the Great Void beyond the void, there is that wonder consisting of the full *ahantā* (I-ness) of Maheśa through the non-duality of "I" and "this"; because knowledge predominates, the aspect of action rests within *ahantā*, and this is the state of Sadāśiva. Herein abide the subjects who are the Mantramaheśvaras.

Likewise, in this very state, that wonder of one's own Self (*svātmacamatkāra*)—in which "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) are held in equilibrium like the pans of a scale through non-differentiation as "I am this"—is His state of Lordship (*īśvarāvasthā*).
Here too, the Mantreśvaras are the subjects (*pramātāraḥ*).

And here too, that wonder consisting of the form "I am I, this is this," in which "I-ness" is predominant and "this-ness" is subordinated, is like the pointing with the head and fingers of a newborn infant; for this alone is the essence of the Blessed One’s consciousness.
The *śuddhavidyā-tattva*.

Here, the seventy million mantras, together with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), exist as the denoters (*vācaka*) by virtue of their nature of grace; they stand toward the Mantra-Maheśvaras and Mantreśvaras, who are the denoted (*vācya*), in order to uplift the bound souls (*paśu*s).

It is proclaimed in the scriptures that although there is no difference in the essential nature of consciousness among the subjects who are the Lords of Knowledge within this *vidyā-tattva*, the manifestation of duality that occurs therein is produced solely by the power of *māyā*.

"Beyond Māyā is Mahāmāyā..."; thus, because the mantras residing there have entered into Mahāmāyā, they are called *aṇus*. Above the principle of Māyā and below Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) are the Vijñānākalas, who are subjects (*pramātṛs*) and the vessel for the *āṇavamala* (the impurity of individuality).

Thus, this single reality, which is the very nature of Śiva, though transcending the fourth state (*turyātīta*), is celebrated as having the form of the fourth state (*turya*) and as the fivefold set of principles (*tattvapañcaka*).

Therefore, this one independent agent alone shines forth; that light which exists on the levels of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—expressed as "I am this"—is itself the instrument consisting of pure consciousness (*śuddhavedana*), while the emanation of the principles beginning with Māyā and ending with Earth is what will be described hereafter.

The effect (*kārya*) is nothing other than the supreme subject (*paramapramātā*), known as the Great Lord of one's own self (*svātmamaheśvara*), who alone unfolds in the form of agent, instrument, and action. // 14 //

He states the essential nature of the principle of Māyā: "That supreme sovereignty of the Great Lord which accomplishes the impossible is the Goddess, the power of Māyā; this is the veil of Śiva over His own Self. (15)

The supreme, absolute sovereignty of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), which is independent of anything else and consists in His being the creator of the universe—that indeed is this power called *māyā* belonging to that possessor of power (*śaktimat*). It is called *māyā* because by it the manifold expansion of subjects and objects (*pramātṛ-prameya-prapañca*) extending down to the earth is measured or delimited; or alternatively, it is *māyā* because of its deluding nature toward the universe. Considering that this belongs to the God whose nature is play (*krīḍā-śīla*), She is the Goddess (*devī*); however, as for the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādins*), no such *māyā* is possible as something separate [from Brahman].
What kind of sovereignty is this, that it is said to "accomplish the difficult-to-accomplish"?
It is the accomplishment—that is, the attainment—of an effect that is difficult to bring about (durghaṭa), namely the subject-object form, which can only be brought about with difficulty.

This very [power] is Māyā; it is the self-concealment of Śiva, who has by his own will entered the state of a bound soul (paśu), known as the hiding of his own nature, consisting of the three impurities beginning with the āṇava. 15.

Regarding the nature of the *puṃstattva* (the principle of the person), which is the subject of experience distinct from the objects of enjoyment—consisting of pleasure and so forth—that will be described later [in the Prādhānika section], he states its essential character:
"Under the influence of the grasping of *māyā*, the consciousness of the person becomes defiled and he becomes a bound soul (*paśu*).
Bound by the power of *kāla*, *kalā*, and *niyati*, and by means of *rāga* and *avidyā*... (16).

Because it is dependent upon the acceptance of *māyā*, consciousness—even though it consists of omniscience and omnipotence—falls into the state of the *āṇava-mala* (the impurity of individuality), which takes the form of non-recognition (*akhyāti*) by casting aside qualities such as omniscience.

By this means, like the space within a jar, it is delimited and rendered finite from the all-pervading space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), and thus it is called the *puṃs-tattva* (the principle of the individual soul).

Therefore, it is a "bound soul" (*paśu*) because it is to be protected and bound by *māyā*; it is the vessel for the fetters (*pāśa*) whose natures are the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* impurities.

Furthermore, the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva) is completely bound—that is, woven together—by the six principles, such as time (kāla) and the rest, whose natures will be described as "the divisions of time" (kālakalā), in a state of being interwoven like warp and woof. Thus is the individual soul enveloped by the six principles. 16.
He now states the essential nature of the principles beginning with *kāla* according to this sequence of envelopment: "I know only this much, and only this very thing, as the self of all.
It is said that this group of six coverings (*kañcuka*), together with *māyā*, constitutes the inner sphere of the individual soul (*aṇu*). (17)

In this way, although consciousness is independent, just as it attains the state of atomicity (*aṇutva*) through its own *māyā*, so too its powers of knowledge and action become contracted; these two [powers] of this [consciousness] in its form as a bound soul (*paśu*) are called *vidyā* and *kalā*.

Just as a small amount of wealth is given for the sake of subsistence out of compassion to one whose entire property has been seized by a king, even so, for consciousness that has attained atomicity and whose omniscience and other qualities have been taken away, the supreme reality of limited agency and knowledge is stimulated; thus, it is [the power] of knowledge itself...
Because of their predominance, time and the other factors have been shown to be connected with the verb "to know.

This aforementioned group of six coverings (kañcukas), conjoined with Māyā in its described form, is said to be the inner, innate obscuration of the individual soul (aṇu)— that person whose omniscience and other qualities have been cast aside by the impurity of finitude (āṇavamala)— just as tarnish is to gold.
He asks, "Of what nature [is this]? and replies with the words beginning "now" (*adhunā*).

Thinking "I know [it] right now," that atom, by virtue of its presentness, delimits even existing things by conceiving them in such a way through the very nature of the act of knowing—as "this was known by me previously," "I know [it]," or "I shall know [it]," and likewise as "I have done," "I am doing," or "I shall do. Thus, he delimits [them].
And this is its "time" (kāla).

Likewise, by saying "only a certain thing," it delimits [its action]; it is not capable of doing everything, but is able to produce only a jar, and not a cloth or other objects—this is the principle of *kalā* for this atom (*aṇu*). By the phrase "this very thing," it seeks a specific effect from a specific cause, such as smoke from fire alone, or the Aśvamedha sacrifice and so forth.

Thus, by the rule that the fruit such as heaven does not arise from every action, the self is constrained by the merits and demerits arising from the continuity of actions performed according to its own volition; that which effects this is its *niyatitattva* (the principle of necessity).

Likewise, "with the whole soul" refers to this sense of incompleteness—the thought "all this is for me," "may I have more," and "may I never cease to exist"—which is the *rāgatattva* (the principle of attachment) of the bound soul (*paśu*).

The passion (*rāga*) which is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) is merely an attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) directed toward a single object characterized as "beloved," while excluding others, thinking "my passion is for this one"; it is not identical to the principle of passion (*rāgatattva*), which consists of a longing for everything.
Likewise, the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*) is that by which one knows only a certain object present before one, such as a jar, and not an object that is distant or concealed;
it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*) in the *Kārikā* with respect to pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), but not because of an absence of cognition.
This group of six coverings (kañcukas), accompanied by Māyā and joined with the manifestation of duality, belongs to the bound soul (paśu). // 17 //
How is it that this sixfold sheath is internal to the individual soul (aṇu)? To this he says:
Like the husk situated upon a grain of rice, it remains undifferentiated even though distinct;
yet it attains purification through the application of being oriented toward the path of Śiva. (18)

Just as a husk, though distinct by its actual nature, appears non-different because it is situated within the grain of rice— so that even when carefully extracted by experts, it does not remain separate due to its internal position within the rice— likewise, this sheath consisting of *māyā* and the rest, being internal to the jewel-like Self which occupies the place of the rice, remains [unperceived].
The remainder [of the meaning] is that even though it is distinct, it remains by concealing the nature of perfect consciousness through its non-distinctness.
Even so, since it is difficult to ward off, he says "it resorts to" (*bhajate*) and so forth to explain how it is dissolved;
the particle *tu* indicates a distinction, for there is no other means in this matter.

The path of Śiva—the Great Lord who is one's own Self—is that way which consists of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the manifestation of the glory of one's own essential nature, namely: "I am this very universe, which is a single mass of supreme non-dual consciousness-bliss; this entire world is merely the unfolding of my own power.
Orientation toward that path—being intent upon contemplating it with firmness—is itself Yoga, in its full form, within the individual soul (*aṇu*) in its own Self.

Through its own essential nature, there is a connection; by that, the aforementioned covering (kañcuka) attains a specific purity and undergoes complete dissolution of its own accord. This is what is meant: when the bound soul (paśu) becomes one whose heart is purified by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (śaktipāta), then [he realizes], "I am indeed the Great Lord."

Thus, through the manifestation of knowledge of one's own self, the covering of the sheaths (kañcuka-āvaraṇa) which brings about the state of being a bound soul (paśu) dissolves by itself; indeed, in this state, apart from the knowledge of one's own self, no other karma arising from the power of Māyā or Niyati has any efficacy. // 18 //

Since such an atom must have an enjoyer and there must be an object of enjoyment, he describes the creation of the principles belonging to primordial matter (pradhāna): "Primordial matter is merely pleasure, pain, and delusion;
then the internal organ, consisting of the intellect, mind, and ego-sense, arises in succession. (19)

That which consists of the common nature (*sāmānya-rūpa*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion—in which no relationship of part and whole (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*) is perceived, is *prakṛti*, the root cause.
Immediately following *prakṛti*, he describes the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its form as an effect, beginning with the word "ascertainment" (*niścaya*).

Ascertainment is the conceptualization that "this is such-and-such"; [then] thinking (*manana*), and then self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and finally the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*)—in this sequence, these are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*).

The triad consisting of the form of "I-making" (ahaṅkāra) and so forth is the internal organ; it is the effect of the guṇas through the relationship of part and whole, and it is the cause in relation to the elements, the senses, and so on. // 19 //

He states the external organs: the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the sense organs (buddhīndriya) with respect to sound and the other objects; furthermore, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are the organs of action (karmendriya). (20)

Regarding the objects to be described, such as sound and so forth, there are the five sense organs—ear and the rest—which have cognition as their primary function, and the five organs beginning with speech which have action as their primary function.
The objects of the organs of action consist of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure.
Thus, because they follow from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) in the form of "I hear" and "I speak," they are the effects of the ego-sense. (20)

He describes the nature of their objects, such as sound and the rest: "The subtle object of these, which is devoid of differentiation, is that pentad of *tanmātras*: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (21)
That which is to be accepted as the object and sphere of these senses, by virtue of being their knowable effect—what is it like?

It is that object which is devoid of differentiation (*pravibhāga-varjita*), specifically excluded from particulars, and is of the nature of the universal (*sāmānyātman*) and subtle; that very thing, such as sound and so forth, in its universal form, is the "merely-that" (*tanmātra*), such as the "sound-merely-that" (*śabda-tanmātra*), and likewise the others.

Because the object and the subject are mutually dependent, this pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) is likewise derived solely from the ego-principle (ahaṅkārika), just like the sense organs. // 21 //
He states that the elements such as earth and the rest constitute the effect through the mutual intermingling of the sense-objects:
"By virtue of this conjunction, the gross object attains the state of the five elements—ether, air, fire, water, and earth. (22)

Through the power of their conjunction and mutual friction, that specific gross object which arises attains the state of the primary elements (*bhūta*). For instance: from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) arises the specific quality of sound, which is space (*nabha*); from sound and touch arise air; from these two when joined with form arises fire; from these when joined with taste arise the waters; and from these when joined with smell arises earth—thus are the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūtāni*).
Considering that the effect conforms to its cause, [the qualities] increase by one at each stage.

Thus, this *prakṛti*, consisting of both cause and effect, has proceeded as an object of experience for the Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, by His will. Having thus divided the universe consisting of thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and described each principle, he states that *prakṛti* acts as a covering (*kañcuka*) for the Puruṣa, just like the coverings of *māyā*.
Just as the husk envelops the grain of rice, so does this creation, preceded by primordial nature (prakṛti),
envelop consciousness down to the level of the earth, assuming the form of the body.

This primary creation, extending down to the earth, is like the husk; just as the husk and the grain-skin envelop and completely cover the grain, so too consciousness (caitanya), already enveloped by the sheath of Māyā which stands in the place of the husk, is further enveloped by the state of embodiment, which stands in the place of the husk, and is thus concealed by it acting as a surrounding wall.

In this context, these subjects (pramātṛ) who possess bodies by virtue of the *kalās*—ranging from the mere sense organs (*indriya*) down to the specific elements (*viśeṣa*)—are called *sakala*. Those devoid of the specific elements, being bodiless, are called *pralayākala*. Thus, the universe is presided over by the sevenfold hierarchy of subjects, beginning with Śiva and ending with the *sakala*, and is governed by Rudras and individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). // 23 //
He describes the nature of the three sheaths as being supreme, subtle, and gross:

"In this system, impurity (mala) is the supreme covering; the sheath of Māyā and the rest is the subtle; and the external form of the body is the gross. Indeed, the Self is enveloped by these three sheaths. (24)

The internal *āṇavamala* (atomic impurity) is the very non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) of the true nature of consciousness, which consists in its casting aside its own essential form; it is the supreme inner veil or covering, like the blackness on gold, because it exists through identity with the Self.

The six sheaths (*kañcukas*), beginning with *māyā* and ending with *vidyā*, constitute the subtle veil of the Self, like the husk of a grain of rice; they remain as a subsequent layer by which the manifestation of knowledge, agency, and so forth, consisting of duality, comes to be spread forth—this is the *māyīyamala* (impurity of Maya).

In relation to this, the external covering—consisting of the primary elements (prādhānika) characterized by the existence of the body and comparable to the husk—is gross, because it takes the form of skin, flesh, and so forth; this is the third impurity, the *kārmamala*, by which the subject becomes a vessel for the accumulation of auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Thus, enveloped by these three sheaths—which exist in the forms of the supreme (*para*), the subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the gross (*sthūla*)—the Self, though expansive like the space within a jar, is contracted and is therefore called an "atom" (*aṇu*) and a "bound soul" (*paśu*). // 24 //
Because of this connection, one becomes as if afflicted; thus he says:
"Due to the conjunction with the darkness of ignorance, one perceives even one's own single nature, the Self, through the manifold variety of the grasped and the grasper. (25)

This Self, bound by the three sheaths, due to its connection with the darkness of the non-apprehension of its own nature, perceives— through a manifold expansion consisting of the various arrangements of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge— its own innate, non-dual, and unitary nature, which is consciousness characterized as self-existence and not derived from anything else; that is to say, it conceives of it through duality, which is the opposite of non-duality.

Just as a person afflicted by the optical disorder *timira*, seeing even a single moon, discerns that "these two moons are in the sky" and shows it to others, saying, "Look, these two moons," while in reality that moon is only one, yet due to the power of *timira* it appears thus; consequently, that person with *timira* undergoes a causal function characterized either by distress or by joy.

In the same way, one who has reached the manifestation of duality through the darkness of ignorance, while dealing with everything as distinct even though it is non-different from his own self, seeks diverse fruits of action by which he repeatedly becomes a partaker of experiences such as heaven and hell;
therefore, ignorance is metaphorically described as "darkness" because it causes things to appear in a distorted manner. // 25 //
He demonstrates the non-duality of the Self through an illustration:
"Just as juice, syrup, granulated sugar, jaggery, candied sugar, and so forth, are nothing but sugarcane juice itself, even so are all the various states of the Supreme Self, Śambhu. (26)
Just as various types of sugarcane, such as *rasālā* and others, are in ultimate reality nothing but the single juice of sugarcane because sweetness permeates them all everywhere,

so too all the distinctions of the waking and other states— which consist of the manifold expansion of the grasped and the grasper— are nothing but the supreme self-nature of Śambhu, the Great Lord of Consciousness, the Supreme Self.

For that very Blessed One, who is the self-nature of all, having entered into various stages through his own sovereignty, manifests as characterized by states such as the grasped and the grasper; yet, just as sugarcane juice does not exist as something separate from its own essence, he is one alone in all states because consciousness persists through them.
Thus, by perceiving this single uniform nature everywhere, the knower becomes all-seeing.
As the venerable Śambhubhaṭṭāraka has said:
"One reality is the essential nature of all realities; all realities have the essential nature of that one reality."
He by whom one entity is seen in its true nature has seen all entities in their true nature.
Thus it is said; and in the Bhagavadgītā as well:
"That knowledge by which one perceives the one undecaying reality in all beings, undivided within the divided—know that to be sāttvika."
Thus [ends verse] 26.
However, the distinctions postulated by other schools, even if accepted for the sake of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), cannot be sustained on the level of ultimate truth (*satya*); thus he says:

"The internal consciousness, the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the cosmic body (*virāḍ-deha*), birth, and the physical aggregate—these are merely conventional designations; in the ultimate sense, they do not exist at all. (27)

The Vijñānavādins maintain that what is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) is merely pure awareness, absolute and devoid of adjuncts (anupādhi), and though free from name-and-form (nāmarūpa), it appears in various ways as external forms such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, through the power of the diversity of the awakening of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). [As it is said:
"All this is indeed the Person (puruṣa)..."

According to the principle that "there is no diversity whatsoever here," the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins) maintain that the Supreme Brahman alone— the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all— manifests as differentiated due to the power of beginningless ignorance (avidyā).
In both of these views, it has not been considered that the autonomy of consciousness (*vedana*), which constitutes its very life, is the cause of the creation of the universe.

Others, however, who are proponents of *prāṇa* as Brahman, maintain that the universe exists by merely breathing; they say with reflection that "there is no form of Brahman other than breathing," and thus declare it to be the *Śabdabrahman*.
Still others hold the view that it is the body of Virāj, asserting that even the cosmic form of Virāj is the true reality of Brahman, as it has been said:
"He whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, and whose feet are the earth."
The sun is his eye, the quarters of space are his ears; homage to him, the self of the worlds!
And so forth.

The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that "genus" (*jāti*)—the general characteristic of great existence (*mahāsattā*), the substrate of all qualities, and the entity that is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Others, however, hold that "individuals" (*piṇḍa*)—that is, the particular manifestations (*vyakti*) alone—are ultimately real, for there is no such thing as a single universal (*sāmānya*) that serves as the substrate of multiple qualities.
The conventional usage regarding individuals is fully exhausted by the statement that "it neither manifests nor is it logically tenable"; thus, what need is there for a universal (*sāmānya*)?

Disputing over the universal through various conceptual constructions regarding its multiple occurrences, they say such things as "individuals do not follow [a common nature], nor does anything else that follows [them] appear.
Speaking much in this manner, they have concluded that the genus (*jāti*) is not an ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, the mass [of cognition] consists of consciousness and so forth.

Those whose distinctions are such [as described] are so called; this is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*). In this doctrine of absolute freedom (*svātantryavāda*), because the manifesting reality cannot be denied, these distinctions appear as conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they do not exist at all.
Thus, these distinctions are not real entities, unlike the distinctions imagined by other philosophical schools which are indeed [considered] existent.

Therefore, there is only one Supreme Lord of Consciousness (*caitanyamaheśvara*), who is the ultimate reality of supreme luminosity and absolute freedom; for he shines forth in this or that manner, since there is no possibility of anything else—distinct from him and of the nature of non-luminosity—being manifest.
As it has been said:
"Whatever those addicted to the teachings of various sects proclaim as 'the reality,' having imagined it through their own intellectual fancies," [that is merely their own fabrication].
That very reality belongs to you; there is nothing else at all—this is merely a dispute among the learned regarding designations.
Thus [ends the twenty-seventh].
Now, he provides an illustration by means of the power of error to produce an unreal object:
"A snake does not exist in a rope, yet it causes terror even unto death;
the power of error is indeed so great that it cannot be [easily] discerned. (28)

The power—the supreme capacity—of error, which consists in the non-apprehension of fullness, to manifest as something that is not of that nature, cannot be distinguished by anyone; that is to say, it cannot be analyzed by anyone. For example, when a rope is actually perceived, due to the delusion of its length and coiled form, it is determined by those who perceive it to be "this is a snake."

Even with respect to the substance of a rope, this determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a snake is a manifestation of a non-existent object; yet, due to the manifestation of that [non-existent] object, it produces fear and leads to the conviction of death.

This is established by experience: who indeed has not undergone the destruction of their heart through the breaking of delusion, having thought a post to be a ghost and having mentally delineated its terrifying form? Such is error (*vibhrama*).
Thus, this is the cause for the manifestation of incompleteness. // 28 //
This establishes the point at hand:

likewise, dharma and adharma, heaven and hell, birth and death, pleasure and pain, as well as the castes, stages of life, and so forth—though non-existent in the Self—come to be through the power of delusion. (29)
Just as a rope, which is real in the ultimate sense, even when perceived through delusion as a snake, performs the causal function (arthakriyā) belonging to a snake,

so too, in the minds of those who identify the body with the self, even that which is non-existent— such as dharma and so forth— is, though not existing in reality, produced by the power of the delusion of māyā; through the error [thinking] "this alone is the truth," it acquires existence.
