Dharma consists of the horse sacrifice and so forth; adharma consists of the killing of a Brahmin and so forth; *svarga* is unsurpassed bliss; *niraya* is torment; *utpatti* is birth; *maraṇa* is death; the absence of birth is [the goal]; pleasure is delight; pain is agitation born of the *rajas* quality; likewise, "color" (*varṇa*) refers to "I am a Brāhmaṇa" and so forth; "stage of life" (*āśrama*) refers to "I am a student" (*brahmacārī*) and so forth; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth," austerity, worship, and vows are included—all this [is sublated].
One falsely identifies with the body and so forth through the power of *māyā*, which is essentially nothing but conceptual construction and a manifestation of delusion.

All this arises from error, by which bound souls (*paśu*) incessantly undergo the continuous succession of births and deaths in heaven and hell; yet, in the ultimate sense, dharma, adharma, and the like do not belong to one's own self, which is a single mass of undivided consciousness and bliss.
"Something exists. // 29 //

Having thus examined the capacity of error (*bhrānti*) in causing the appearance of non-existent objects, he describes its arising: "This is that darkness which, even though things are not distinct from the self, produces this conceit of a non-self (*anātma-abhimāna*) regarding them as if they were appearing [as external]. (30)

"This is that darkness" refers to this very delusion just explained— the universal deluder consisting of the non-recognition of fullness— which exists in all objects throughout the universe in the form of subjects and objects of knowledge as they manifest;
for "that which is not light does not shine."
Thus, although these entities have become the very body of manifestation— being inseparable from the Great Lord’s consciousness (caitanya) of the Self—
and exist as such, there arises this conceit of non-self (*anātmābhimāna*) which, by way of excess, regards them as objects of perception, external, and distinct from oneself;
this consists in casting off their true nature as consciousness and thereby attributing to them an unreal state of insentience (*jaḍatva*).

This is the intended meaning [of Utpaladeva] in the *Bhāvaprakāśana*: since no other cause—such as external latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or the like—which is of the nature of non-manifestation, is logically tenable, it follows that the manifestation of one's own self (*svātmaprakāśa*) alone, being independent, manifests as objects such as blue or pleasure; therefore, in its true nature, it is "I myself," the very essence of consciousness, who am the manifestation in the form of both subject and object. Thus, that which is the real nature does not manifest; rather, it is only unreal duality that appears.
Thus, because there is no manifestation of reality, error is metaphorically described as darkness. // 30 //

Demonstrating that the conceit of self in what is not-self is preceded by the conceit of non-self in the self, he declares the nature of this delusion to be even more profound than mere blindness: "This is a darkness even greater than cataracts; this is a great boil upon a tumor:
that there is the conceit of self even in what is not-self, such as the body and the vital breath. (31)

First of all, even among entities whose true nature is a single consciousness, a state of insentience consisting of differentiation has been produced by the darkness of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). This is because entities that are non-different from one's own self manifest as distinct from it; for this very reason, non-apprehension is like a "darkness," just as the moon, though one, appears as two—"two moons"—due to the darkness of a streak in the eye. In the same way, through the darkness of non-apprehension, every object, though its true nature is the one Self, manifests as differentiated and as having the nature of a non-self.
It has been illuminated.

Such being the case, this further darkness has arrived; through delusion, this further delusion has fallen, like the appearance of a carbuncle upon a boil, since even while all things existing in the universe—whose true nature as consciousness has been cast aside by non-apprehension—have been rendered inert, that which was extracted from their midst [is now obscured].

To conceive as the Self that which is not the Self—namely, the inert, objective, and fragmented body, vital breath, and so forth, regarding which one thinks "I am thin," "I am fat," "I am hungry," "I am happy," or "I am nothing"—while these are objects of cognition and not the subject, is a most grievous error (*ativaiśasam*).

If such a grievous error could exist even without the conceit of being the Self, then let it apply equally to blue, pleasure, and the like; or else, let it not apply to anything at all. However, [the case is different] when...

Some dull-witted people, regarding the body and so forth—which are like clods of earth—as the Self, perform anointing with the essence of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*); elsewhere, they establish as non-Self things such as blue objects or pleasure through the notion of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

This alone is the full extent of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is to be lamented, for it is by being subjected to the conceit [of this] that the blow of dualities drags away the bound souls (*paśu*).
As it was said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* by the yoginī Madālasā:
The vehicle is on the ground, yet the body is situated within the vehicle; and within the body, another—the Puruṣa—is established.
One does not possess such a sense of "mine" toward the earth as one does toward one's own body, and this excessive attachment is sheer delusion.
Thus [ends verse] 31.
Thus, due to non-apprehension, one binds oneself in this way through false conceptualizations; so it is said:
"By means of the expansion of the body, vital breath, reflection, intellect, knowledge, and space, one envelops oneself in a manifold way, like a spider with its web. (32)
Every cognizer, whose consciousness has been cast aside by non-apprehension (akhyāti), binds himself—though he is all-pervasive—with the shackles of his own conceptual constructions (vikalpa).
To explain how this occurs, [the author] says "the body," and so forth.

Through the connection with the body and other such constructs—that is, through the association with the conceptualization of the body and so on—there arises the discernment of the body and vital breath, the cognition of the intellect, the determination [of objects], and the expansion of the manifold of space.

Just as children, women, commoners, and farmers—considering themselves somewhat discerning—regard the body alone as the self through their own conceptual construction, thinking, "I am thin," "I am stout," "I am beautiful," or "I am learned"; [the author replies:

the body, however, perishes right here; how, therefore, can it be the self? Furthermore, those who consider themselves even more discerning than the former, yet who identify the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the self, think, "I am he who is hungry" or "I am he who is thirsty."

"The body and the vital breath are insentient like a clod of earth; how, then, could they possess the nature of the Self? Therefore, that which perceives pleasure, pain, and so forth—thinking 'I am happy' or 'I am miserable'—is the Self. Thus argue the Mīmāṃsakas and others who identify with the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), as well as those most skilled in discrimination. [To this we reply: even this pleasure, pain, and so forth are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*); how can it be possible to describe them as the Self? Therefore, "that wherein there is the absence of the conceptualizations of body, vital breath, and intellect is the Self"—so say those who identify with the Void (*śūnya*).

Thus, whatever appears here, being of a nature that is not manifested as "I," is indeed emptiness (*śūnya*) whose very essence is the exclusion of everything; this is what is designated by the term "space" (*nabhas*).

When, at the time of meditative absorption, one makes even that emptiness an object of awareness, thinking, "We are not even this emptiness," then, by abandoning each respective emptiness accepted by the proponents of Brahman through the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), one establishes another emptiness as the Self.
The elaboration regarding space (*nabhaḥ-prapañca*) has been described in the *Kārikā* as "grasping at this or that state of emptiness.

Thus, because they do not reach the true nature of consciousness (*saṃvit-svarūpa*), those yogins who conceive of themselves as empty and are submerged in the cave of deep sleep are indeed deluded and inert; they mistakenly bind even the nature of consciousness itself with inertia.
It is truly a wonder—and a tragedy—that they are unable to realize for themselves that "this [consciousness] cannot be made so by anyone else."
Regarding this, he states an illustration beginning with "by a web" (*jālena*),

and so forth: just as a certain spider or insect, having fashioned a web— a covering— out of its own saliva or froth, envelops itself on all sides and binds itself for its own destruction, whereby it subsequently meets its end right there.

In the same way, one who identifies the body and so forth as the self binds his very own self through conceptual constructions of "I" and "mine" imagined by his own discursive thought. And thus the Buddhists [teach]: "When there is a self, there is the notion of 'other'; from the division of self and other arise attachment and aversion."
All defects arise when these two are conjoined.
Thus they say. // 32 //

"How is this insurmountable great delusion—which arises from the sense of being a limited subject centered on the body and so forth—dissolved? To this, he says that the Lord's very sovereignty is the cause here:
"By means of the yoga of manifesting the power of his own consciousness, he should unravel his own self;
thus does Supreme Śiva extend the variegated play of bondage and liberation. (33)

The "vibhava" (manifestation) of the knowledge of one's own self—which is characterized by consciousness and consists in the realization of one's own sovereignty—is the expansion of that sovereignty within the nature of pure consciousness, occurring through the dissolution of the conceit of the body and so forth; it is the state of the supreme "I-consciousness" (*parāhaṃtā*) as a wonder, the solid mass of the unity of consciousness and bliss, and the awareness:
"I am independent. The manifestation, or the light, of this *vibhava*—which is the very nature of the sovereignty of awakening—is everything.

The *yoga* is precisely the appropriation within one's own self of everything regarded as external, thinking "this is mine. Through this process of constant cultivation, the firmness of one’s self-awareness (*vimarśa*) within the Self is established. By means of this application of the manifestation of the glory of one’s own knowledge, one unravels one’s own innate nature—which is consciousness itself and not something acquired from elsewhere—from the fetters consisting of the identification with the body, the vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void.

He was enveloped; yet, through the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that "I am independent and of the nature of consciousness," the Lord Himself once again effects the unbinding, making it free from the envelopment.

Thus, the obscuration of one's own self by the body and so forth, which arose through the power of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), perishes again through the power of recognition (*khyāti*). Therefore, this much is the defect imagined by one's own conceptual construction—so it was stated by the venerable author of the *Tantrasāra*.
The dull conviction of the worldly person— that "I am inert, I am bound by karma, I am impure, I am driven by others"—
is instantly transformed into the state of being the Lord, the conscious Self whose body is the universe, through the method of attaining this other firm conviction.
Thus [it is asked]: "Why does the Blessed One bind and why does he release? To this he says: "Binding," and so forth.

According to the sequence previously established, the Blessed One—Paramaśiva, who is independent and characterized by the single, dense mass of perfect consciousness and bliss—because his nature is to sport in the concealment of his own essence, first brings about the manifestation of non-recognition (*akhyāti*) and then makes his very self assume the state of a subject (*pramātṛ*) consisting of the body and so forth.

Having assumed His own nature and concealed His bondage, He likewise brings it about again by His own will; and by the process of illuminating the knowledge of His own Self, having removed the bondage of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) consisting of the body and so forth, He alone liberates that very Self. Thus, in both ways—through bondage and liberation—He expands and extends this wondrous play and sport, which consists of the marvelous nature of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) and liberation (apavarga), thinking: "I do not delight in being alone."
This is indeed the very nature of the Lord: that even when he has entered into various states, being his own essential form, he manifests everywhere as the experiencer; this alone is his sovereignty.
Not only this, but the Lord manifests every other particular state as well, resting precisely within its own form; thus he says:
"Creation, maintenance, and dissolution, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—all these shine within that fourth abode (turiya), yet even so, it shines unobscured by them. (34)

All emanations and so forth that exist in relation to the universe, as well as the specific states such as waking and so on that reside within the illusory subject— both of these shine within this Lord, the fourth abode, which is a mass of bliss; resting therein, they obtain their own ontological existence as something external in relation to the imagined subject.
That which does not shine upon the background of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) does not shine even as something external; therefore, "the fourth [state] should be poured like oil into the three.
This is the ultimate truth: that in all states, the form of the Fourth (turya) remains as the underlying thread.
To the question of whether their own nature (*svarūpa*) has been concealed therein by those [limitations] to such an extent, he says: "Nevertheless, it shines forth unobscured by them.

Even though its existence as its own nature is thus obscured by them, because it has transcended them and is the universal experiencer, it manifests everywhere; yet, due to that obscuration, its full nature does not remain hidden there. This is the abode of Śiva (*śivadhāma*).
It is always completely full, even in all states. // 34 //
By means of the terminology of Vedānta, while describing the nature of the three states beginning with waking—which are interwoven within it—it reveals that which is beyond them, the Fourth (turya):
"The waking state is Viśva due to differentiation; the dream state is Taijasa because of the majesty of its light;
the deep sleep state is Prājña because of the density of consciousness; beyond that is the Fourth. (35)

The waking state itself is the universe, the *vairāja* nature of Brahman. Why? Because of differentiation: since the fivefold objects such as sound and so forth—created by the Supreme Lord as external—are the very objects toward which the eyes and other senses of all subjects proceed, there arises a manifold variety of sensory cognitions within that single Brahman who exists in the relationship of subject and object.
Therefore, in the Śivasūtras it is said:
"Knowledge is the waking state.
This is celebrated as the *virāj* state of Brahman.
As the Śruti says: "He who is all-seeing, indeed whose face is on every side, whose hands are on every side, and whose feet are on every side—
he, the one God, generating heaven and earth, stretches them out with his arms and wings."
Thus, dream is the state of fire (tejas) of Brahman.
Why? He says: "Because of the majesty of light.
In a dream, the external organs do not exert their power over objects such as sound, nor is there any external sound or the like therein.

In ultimate reality, not even the slightest thing exists as such; nor, when examined through reasoning, is any other cause—whether distinct or non-distinct from ignorance and so forth—perceived or logically tenable for the determination of externality. And yet, everything manifests in a dream;
therefore, by the force of this fact, it follows that the Lord himself, the Divine whose nature is his own self, assumes those various states of subjectivity.

Pervaded [by the Supreme Lord] and as if dreaming, He Himself, through the freedom of His own light, divides Himself into the manifold variety of subjects such as houses, cities, and towers; thus, for each subject, He manifests the universe as something unique to that dreamer.
Therefore, the freedom of Brahman is accepted by the proponents of Brahman (Brahmavādins) in the very state of dreaming.
For this is stated in the Vedantas: "Having divided himself by himself and created various kinds of beings,
the Lord of All, who consists of all things, appears as the enjoyer in a dream."
Thus, the very majesty of manifestation is the cause here; therefore, dream is the state of Brahman’s *tejas*.
Likewise, the *prājña* is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
That which is the state of deep sleep for all subjects—that is the *prājña*; thus, the *prājña* state is the state of Brahman.

For, when the proliferation of the grasped and the grasper has dissolved for all subjects, in that state of deep sleep—which is of the nature of the Great Void (*mahāśūnyatva*), wherein the grasped and so forth have vanished leaving only residual impressions (*saṃskāra*)—the consciousness (*prajñā*) of Brahman itself, which is the seed of the universe, remains as the innermost knower of Brahman; this is what is meant.

This very state is the ground of impressions (*saṃskārabhūmi*) from which the manifestation of the entire variety of the universe, such as blue, pleasure, and so on, arises for every subject upon awakening.

Because we observe that worldly discourse proceeds as if [the Self] were previously experienced; otherwise, if Brahman—which is stable, of the nature of the knower, and inclusive of everything—had not been manifested on this ground [of deep sleep], how could there arise for the cognizer who has arisen from it a memory of that very thing as "it was thus," characterized by its having been previously experienced? Nor would there arise the recollections, "I slept happily" or "I slept painfully."
"The experience 'I was profoundly deluded' would have manifested";
and likewise, as Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa [argued]:
"If all experienced objects were not secured within you, having been assimilated into your own self."
If it were so, then no such thing as memory—which consists in the non-forgetting of a cognized object—could possibly exist.
Thus, deep sleep is proclaimed to be the state of the *prājña* (the conscious one), which is indeed Brahman consisting of consciousness alone.
Why? Because of its being a mass of knowledge (*jñānaghana*).
This reason, being common to both deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*), should be applied to both.

This is the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptabhūmi*), a mass of consciousness whose form is light; yet, being merely obscured by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the dissolution of the universe, it does not become pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmayī*).
As it is said in the *Spandaśāstra*:
"Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge..."
The pervasive Lord shines in two ways: as the manifest world and, elsewhere, as pure consciousness.
Thus: "Beyond that is the Fourth (turya).

Therefore, beyond deep sleep (suṣupta), there is another state called the Fourth form of Brahman, which consists of pure, perfect bliss due to the complete exhaustion of all latent impressions and tendencies of bondage. Since no other name here is appropriate to its meaning, it is the place of rest for the three previously explained states.

It is said to be "interwoven" (*anusyūta*) by virtue of being the most intimate within all things. Here, the designation of number is made through the ordinal suffix (*pūraṇapratyaya*), calling it the "fourth" (*turya*) because it completes the number four.
To the question of how this can be beyond the three states even while being interwoven with them, he says: "because it is a mass of consciousness" (*jñānaghanatvāt*).

Since all states such as waking and the rest consist of ignorance for perceivers due to their tendency toward duality, whereas the fourth state—because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the agitation between the grasped and the grasper have been utterly destroyed—is the very embodiment of the light and bliss of a mass of consciousness, it remains within those [other states] despite being beyond them.
Because it has transcended those states by virtue of its consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), it is "other" than them—that is, supreme.
Thus, Brahman alone, which is independent, whose nature is supreme non-duality, and which manifests in various states, unfolds as the fullness. // 35 //

Even so, because the pure Supreme Self abides as the thread running through all subjects, one might think that the impurity of non-recognition (*akhyāti*) residing within the multitude of subjects necessarily accrues to It; to show that this is not the case, he provides an illustration:
"Just as the expanse of the sky is not defiled by clouds, smoke, or dust, even so the Supreme Person remains untouched by the transformations of *māyā*. (36)

Just as the surface of the sky, though clouds, smoke, and masses of dust remain within it, is not rendered impure by its very nature— nor is its eternal vastness ever diminished— but remains always the sky itself, being recognized as such despite appearing diverse through various states like reflections in a mirror; so too is the case here.

"In that same way" means that even by the transformations of *māyā*—namely, the various modifications arising from non-recognition (*akhyāti*) which reside in manifold subjects and consist of many diverse states such as birth and death, though these abide in the Lord—the Lord is not touched; His essential nature is not taken away by them. Because He is the Supreme Person (*paraḥ puruṣaḥ*), the primordial manifestation and the place of rest for all persons—that is, all individual souls (*jīvas*)—He shines eternally as the universal experiencer; thus He is designated by the word "Supreme" (*para*).

Therefore, there is no impairment whatsoever of the Blessed One by the transformations of *māyā*—which are non-luminous in nature and arise from Himself—just as in the case of a magician; for this reason, it was stated by Parameṣṭhin in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:

"Although the stability of objects is restricted to the *jīva*, who is constrained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), even there it is established in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."
How could there be for him any restraint by means of the vital breath, since that [restraint] would exist only through his own self?
Thus [it is said]. // 36 //

But if all persons have as their ultimate reality only a single consciousness, how is it that they experience the manifold diversity of various states such as specific pleasure, pain, delusion, birth, and death? To answer this, he provides an illustration:
"Just as when the space within one jar is pervaded by dust, the others do not become soiled; likewise, these individual souls (jīvas) experience the distinctions of pleasure and pain. (37)

Just as when the space within one jar is covered by a heap of dust, the other spaces within jars do not become soiled or covered with dust despite being equally pure, because there is no difference in their nature as space; for although the sky is pure, all-pervading, and eternal, it appears contracted according to the contraction of the jar, yet that [contraction] belongs only to that specific jar, and not all the spaces within jars, cloths, and so forth, are fumigated with black aloe-wood incense.

Perfumed with musk and possessing the scent of camphor, these [spaces] appear as if they were one with space because of their nature as mere space, yet they are distinguished by the delimitations created by the jars and other objects contained within them.
On the contrary, even when the real sky exists as one, jars and other things—being constrained by the contraction of the walls inherent within them—manifest a diversity of various skies.

Thus, it is precisely the contraction produced by the jar that is thus specified as "space," because it performs causal function (*arthakriyā*) by virtue of being such [a contracted space]. It is not [the universal space itself].

Furthermore, just as this slight impurity residing within a jar serves to conceal the true nature of the sky, nor do the spaces of the sky delimited by various jars like pots become intermingled with one another;

in that same way, these individual souls (*jīvas*) or persons, although their ultimate reality is nothing but pure consciousness, are nonetheless enveloped by the three sheaths— the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *prākṛta*— through the power of the supreme Lord’s *māyā*.

Having cast aside its own nature—which is full, all-pervasive, and a single compact mass of consciousness-bliss—by which [ignorance] even those whose essence is the one Consciousness are rendered limited;

and due to the wretchedness of being severed from their own three internal sheaths (kośas), they appear mutually distinct, like the spaces within a jar or a cloth. Thus, it is only this separation created by the sheath of Māyā that is conventionally designated as "jīva-hood"; it is not the case, as seen in other philosophical systems, that there are individual souls (jīvas), persons (puruṣas), or selves (ātmanas) that are atomic (aṇu) within the Supreme Lord, who is an undivided, single compact mass of consciousness-bliss.
Such is the conventional usage.

Thus, individual souls (jīvas), delimited by the sheaths beginning with the food-sheath (annamaya-kośa), being perfumed by the impressions of various karmic impurities from time immemorial, possess diverse bodies, diverse dispositions, and partake in the various dualities of merit and demerit, heaven and hell, pleasure and pain, birth and death, and so forth; yet they do not [confuse] one another.

Just as spaces delimited by jars and other objects—though perfumed by various substances—are perceived as mixed together, it is well-established that even those whose ultimate reality is nothing but a single consciousness appear to possess mutual difference due to their own limitations. // 37 //
Thus, those specific states residing within the circle of living beings are merely metaphorically attributed to the Blessed One, but in reality, none of them exist here in him.
He says: "When he is tranquil, he appears as if tranquil; when joyful, he appears joyful; when deluded, he appears deluded.
While the collection of [mental] factors exists, the Blessed One appears thus, yet in the ultimate sense, he is not so. (38)

When the group of principles—the collection of the senses—is stilled and ceased, the Supreme Self residing therein is considered "stilled" as if it were destroyed; likewise, when that [body] is delighted and full of joy, He is similarly designated as such. Furthermore, when it is deluded and filled with darkness, He is regarded as being "deluded.
Yet, in reality, according to the actual state of things, the Supreme Lord does not truly become so in that manner.

For every insentient portion is subject to arising or to being withdrawn; however, in the Lord, whose nature is consciousness and who abides within the sheaths of *māyā* and so forth, there can be neither destruction nor origination. Thus, the Lord is eternally equal. (38)
The delusion that arose through the process of origination is further utterly uprooted by the process of re-cognition; thus, it is the sovereignty of one's own self that is expressed here:
"Having first dispelled that appearance of the form of [the object] even within what is not the self, the Supreme Self shatters the delusion of the form of the non-self within the self. (39)

That which is the manifestation of forms—such as "I am thin" or "I am fat"—regarding the body and so forth, which are non-self and characterized by insentience, is the conceptualization of the non-self as the self;

having previously, at the very outset, rejected that, one becomes the Self itself, with the bonds of the body dissolved, through the flash of unartificial *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), thinking: "I am a single mass of consciousness and bliss, whose nature is unlimited and autonomous," thereby stripping away the artificial subjectivity of the body and such.

Having attained the state of the Supreme Self, he shatters—that is, grinds to powder—the delusion that arises from the conceit of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) regarding this very self, which is the manifesting form of all worldly objects and whose nature is light; though these objects are like his own limbs, he destroys that perception of duality born from such conceit by realizing: "I alone shine forth as the soul of the universe."

The essential point here is this: as long as the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) regarding the non-self, such as the body and so forth, has not dissolved, so long will the delusion of the manifestation of duality (*bhedaprathāmoha*) not vanish, even within the world which is in reality the manifestation of one's own Self. Therefore, through the destruction of the error of conceiving the non-self as the self, the Supreme Self alone—the Blessed Lord, the Great Master of His own Self—destroys the delusion of conceiving the Self as the non-self; no one else possesses the power for this. 39.
Thus, for the yogin who has become the Supreme Goddess through the removal of these two types of delusion, no further task remains; as it is said:

"In this way, for the supreme yogin who has accomplished his purpose by severing the very root of the pair of delusions, there never arises the notion that any further duty remains to be performed. (40)

In this manner, by the method set forth in the meaning of the *kārikā*, for one who has accomplished their purpose through the full realization of their own sovereignty— which tears asunder the growth of the two-fold delusion— and who has thus attained the goal (*artha*) consisting of the acquisition of the supreme human aim (*puruṣārtha*),
there is never any further duty to be performed, such as visiting sacred sites, occupying holy fields, initiation, recitation, meditation, exposition, or listening to teachings.
There is not even the mental activity of calculating what remains to be done;

this alone is the supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga. Thus, because of the primacy of yoga directed toward one's own Self, there is no further exertion elsewhere for the perfected yogi. As it has been said:
When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion,
then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
Thus it is said in the Gītās. // 40 //

Having now described how the universe— which, from earth up to Māyā, partakes in the manifestation of duality— attains a state of non-duality by dissolving duality through entry into the Śākta stage consisting of both difference and non-difference, and thereby achieving absorption into the Śāmbhava state which is a mass of full light and bliss;
[the author proceeds] thereafter, from that Śāmbhava state which is like a perfect ocean of nectar, beginning with the surging manifestation of the Śākta flow resembling a great torrent.

Intending to gradually unfold the heart of supreme consciousness—which consists of the identity of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva; which is the essence of the potency of the Great Mantra established by one’s own experience; and which is the emergence of supreme non-duality through the dissolution of all duality—he first states the unification of the universe through the logic of synthesizing its nature as the three sections of the Āgama:
"Earth, Prakṛti, and Māyā—this triad has fallen into the state of being an object of knowledge."
Indeed, through the power of the contemplation of non-duality, there remains only pure Being.

That which consists of the cosmic eggs (aṇḍa) of the earthly, the elemental, and the illusory—possessing the threefold nature of gross, subtle, and supreme, and having fallen into the state of being an object of knowledge and thus entered the sphere of cognition—shines forth externally and internally through that very form as knowledge.
Apart from knowledge, there is no existence of objects; therefore, the universe is of the nature of knowledge.
For no entities have ever been made objects by anyone apart from cognition;
therefore, it is concluded that cognition has attained the nature of those very entities.

Thus, by the principle stated in the *Śrīkālikākrama*, that which is the contemplation of non-duality (*advaitabhāvana*), through its power and through its intensification, results in the remainder of pure Being (*sanmātra*), which consists of mere existence (*sattāmātra*) characterized by luminosity.
The particle *hi* is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*). // 41 //

He establishes this very point with the intention of demonstrating that difference is unreal: "Just as gold is seen when the distinctions of the girdle, earring, and bracelet are set aside, so too, when difference is set aside, everything appears as pure Being alone. (42)

Just as, for example, a golden ornament such as a girdle appears merely as gold to one seeking gold, while it appears as mere metal to one seeking only metal— such as gold, silver, bronze, copper, or lead— likewise, for one who has abandoned the stains of conceptual constructions such as rejection and acceptance and who rests solely in non-conceptual appearance,
the accomplishment of that [result] occurs through the transformation of form and the other [sensory objects].
Thus, according to the principle stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa, when duality is abandoned, that which is pure Being, whose essence is mere existence, shines forth. // 42 //

Therefore, having set aside the appearance of contraction for all of this, and by means of the authority of scripture, he speaks while casting a glance toward the tradition of mantra—the ascent of the human form into the Śākta form:
"That supreme Brahman is pure, tranquil, non-dual in nature, equal, and all-encompassing;
it is immortal and true, and it comes to rest in Śakti, whose nature is luminosity. (43)
All this, whose nature is pure existence, is Brahman because of its vastness;
as those who know the Upanishads say: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

Thus, because it is full, it is supreme; because there is an absence of anything to be rejected or accepted, it is pure; because of the subsiding of separateness, it is tranquil; for that very reason, its nature is non-dual; because there is an absence of excellence or deficiency, it is equal;
and even a single location of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization.
Thus, remaining as the whole, it is therefore immortal and indestructible.
In every entity, two parts—the real and the unreal—are established;
therein, that which is real is the universal (jāti), while the unreal are the situated particulars (vyakti).

Thus, according to the principle established by the venerable Bhartṛhari— that "whatever is at the beginning, whatever is at the end, and whatever is in the middle, that is the Truth"— that very Truth, which consists of pure existence (*sattāmātrātmaka*), is all this [universe] within the Supreme [Consciousness], which is of the nature of light and consists of the equilibrium of the powers (*śakti*) of will, knowledge, and action.
"The determination of objects rests upon consciousness when it finds repose in its own power";
according to this principle, one becomes identical with that [consciousness].

And yet, it is peaceful: that which is the cerebral form at the end of the letter *śa*, beyond which lies the immortal—the Brahman whose nature is the seed-syllable of immortality (*amṛtabīja*), consisting of pure existence (*sanmātra*). It is pure through contact with the state called *Sādākhya*; therefore, it is "equal" (*sama*) because of the equalization of all things as "I am all this," and it is "entire" (*sakala*) and "true" (*satya*) because of the dissolution of all designations (*ākhyāti*).
"That which was taught by the Blessed One as the third Brahmā, O lady of beautiful hips...
thus it is said in the *Śrītriṃśikā*.
This very Brahman, which is the self of the universe, touched by the state of immortality and ascended to the station of Sadāśiva, comes to rest within the previously mentioned Śakti. // 43 //
He says that whatever does not rest within the supreme power (para-śakti) by way of action, knowledge, and will is nothing at all:
"It is desired," "it is known," and "it is accomplished"—thus [it exists] as a luminous form;
however, even that which is not so perceived reaches the state of being like a flower in the sky. (44)

Whatever object, though existing externally according to the nature of things, is not grasped by that consciousness—which is radiant, consisting of the expansion of the Supreme Power (parāśakti) characterized by the equilibrium of these three powers (icchā, jñāna, and kriyā)—is devoid of both perception and description, and is like a flower in the sky.
By this, the potency of the state (vṛtti) consisting of the trident situated above the state of existence (sadvṛtti) is indicated. // 44 //
Reiterating this penetration into the state of Śakti, [the Lord] brings about the manifestation of becoming one with that through the attainment of the state of Śambhu;
by means of the union that encompasses the trident of Śakti, everything is also dissolved into the Supreme Lord, the ultimate reality named Śiva, by the God of gods. (45)

Thus, this entire universe, being of the nature of pure existence (*sattāmātra*), is its ultimate reality as the aforementioned Brahman; through the application of the logic established by the union with the trident of power (*śakti-śūla*) and by the process of absorption into the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), it is emitted into one's own essential nature— the Supreme Lord named Śiva, who is the undivided mass of consciousness and bliss, the ultimate reality— and by means of the excellence of inward-facing reflective awareness (*vimarśana*), it is brought to a state of identity with Him through that absorption.
For the gods, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva, as well as for all the luminous senses, the agency belongs solely to the Lord, Paramaśiva;
indeed, the agency of any other whatsoever is not possible here, nor is there any other subject (pramātṛ) distinct from Him.
It is the manifestation of this very Blessed One, as He ascends through various stages, that appears in the form of those respective subjects such as Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas).
The statement "by the God of Gods" is indeed appropriate;
thus has the function of emission (visarga) been demonstrated. // 45 //

Thus, having demonstrated through the perspective of the final synthesis how this world—consisting of differentiated human forms—attains a state of identity with Śiva, the undifferentiated mass of consciousness, by being superposed upon the Śākta plane which is of the nature of both difference and non-difference; [the author now states: it is Śiva alone, who is a single mass of consciousness, who, having manifested in the form of Śakti, flashes forth as the universal form consisting of human beings; for there is no form of Śakti or of humans whatsoever apart from Śiva, since it is Śiva himself who, through his own inherent essence, remains thus condensed.
"It throbs" indicates the principle of expansion consisting of the expansion of the Great Mantra;
furthermore, by means of the sequence of the expansion of the five powers, that [expansion] also occurs externally.
The three variegated eggs (aṇḍas) are emitted externally through the attainment of its own nature. (46)

Paramaśiva is the essence of the equilibrium of the five powers known as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). By means of the method of unfolding the stages called Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā—which consist in the manifestation of the predominance of these powers such as consciousness—he has created that variegated triad of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) in the form of various worlds and so forth, through the externalization of his own self by way of attaining an external nature. This is effected by the manifestation of his own self as having the nature of external appearance.

Furthermore, by the word "again" (punarapi), he shows this: that Supreme Śiva alone, being autonomous, eternally performs the play of manifesting and dissolving the manifold universe upon his own screen;
though not distinct from his own self, he displays it as if it were distinct, remaining thus in this manner, for there is nothing whatsoever existing apart from him. // 46 //
Anticipating the doubt as to who this Lord Śiva is— designated as such because he delights in the play of manifesting and dissolving the universe—

where he resides, and by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) he is established, [the author] demonstrates through words denoting the word "we" (*asmad-śabda*) that Śiva is indeed one's own self (*svātman*). As one's own self, manifesting everywhere as primordially established, he performs the acts of creation and so forth.
Thus, the Lord, driving the machine of the wheel of powers through the yoga of play, [declares]:
"I alone am the pure form, established in the station of the leader of the great wheel of powers. (47)
The entire universe shines within me alone, like jars and other objects in a stainless mirror; everything emanates from me, like the manifold variety of a dream from one who sleeps.
I alone am the universal form; like the body whose nature consists of hands, feet, and so forth, I alone manifest within all things, like luminosity within objects. (49)
Though devoid of body and senses, I alone am the seer, the hearer, and the smeller; though a non-doer, I myself compose the various established doctrines, scriptures, and reasonings.

In the manner thus explained, the Lord—whose essence is the wonder of supreme subjectivity (*parāhaṃtā*), whose nature is the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) consisting of the thought "I am indeed all living beings"—operates by means of the play of union that very machine which is the infinite multitude of powers projected by the fivefold power beginning with consciousness (*cid-ādi*). Turning it around according to the sequence of effortless emergence and submergence in creation and so forth, following the logic of the waterwheel (*araghaṭṭaghaṭīyantra*), he revolves it. He is the one who, as the "I," impels that machine.
This very self-reflection (*svātmaparāmarśa*) is that which cannot be denied by anyone; it is this very Self as God (*deva*), whose nature is to play, who shines forth.
By this it is established that Śiva is indeed grounded in his own essential nature (*svasvarūpaniṣṭha*).
Likewise, "pure in form" means that his sphere of experience transcends all conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Furthermore, that which bestows upon the powers—the deities of the instruments (karaṇas)—the sovereignty over activities such as the grasping and abandoning of objects is the station of the Lord of the Great Wheel (mahācakranāyakapada); he dwells there, being "stationed therein" (tatstha).

Since the powers of the instruments possess no existence in their own right apart from repose in consciousness, they incessantly resort to the Possessor of Power (śaktimant) alone in order to attain their true nature. By this, [it is shown] that because the Blessed One is the presiding authority within the hearts of all subjects...
The notion that [the Lord] is the presiding deity over fixed worlds has been refuted.

Likewise, whatever is considered as the universe, all of that shines within me alone according to the analogy of a reflection in a mirror; it appears as resting solely upon the "I" (asmadartha) whose nature has already been explained, meaning it vibrates as having the essence of "I-ness" (ahantā).

In the same way, from Me—meaning from my own Self in the form of the "I" as the Full (pūrṇa)—this entire universe issues forth without remainder; that is, it manifests as if it were withdrawn from the perspective of the limited subject.

How so? He says: "like the variety of a dream from one who is asleep. Just as for a sleeping subject, in the state of dreaming, there appears a manifold wonder such as cities, walls, and temples—even though external objects are absent—the variety of dream-objects has its material cause solely in one's own consciousness, since no other cause imagined through ignorance and the like exists.
In the same way, the universe proceeds from that single, undivided mass of consciousness and bliss in the form of "I," because other causes restricted by other systems of doctrine are untenable;
thus, [it is said] "I alone am the universal form," and so forth.

This very full awareness of consciousness which is "I" is indeed myself, having assumed the state of various subjects such as bodies and the like, appearing as the universe because it flashes forth with internal differentiation within everyone from cowherds and children to women and others.
The phrase "my very forms" means this:

what is it like? It is like the body, whose nature consists of hands, feet, and so forth; just as, in a general sense, there is one body for all that possesses the nature of hands, feet, and so on, yet it appears in various forms according to the specific characteristics of each individual perceiver, in the same way, the single reality characterized by consciousness is of universal form (*viśvarūpa*) because it is the abode of all.

Thus, in this entire world consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, it is I alone who shine forth, because I manifest as the self-experiencing subject of everything.

How so? "Like a luminous form among objects. Just as a luminous object, characterized by an excellence of radiance, shines intensely among various things, even so am I the one whose nature is consciousness within this inert universe.

Therefore, [the text] says "the Seer" and so forth: although devoid of body and senses, because my form is consciousness (*cinmūrtatvāt*), it is I alone who see, hear, smell, taste, and touch, for there is a resting in the fullness of *ahantā* (I-consciousness) everywhere; thus, one has achieved all that is to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*).

Indeed, the aggregate of body and senses thinks "I see" and so forth, but since the state of being a seer and so on is absent during states such as deep sleep, therefore, the Supreme Person (*paraḥ puruṣa*) alone—expressed by the word "I"—is the one who causes the manifestation of the aggregate of body, senses, and so forth, yet remains devoid of them, being a single mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaikaghana*), moving within the hearts of all beings, and the enjoyer of the experience of objects.
And so says the Śruti:
"Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears.
He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of Him. Him they call the foremost, the Great Person."

Thus, although the Siddhāntāgama and so forth are likewise not created by an external agent, yet—being permeated by the intentions of gods, sages, humans, and others—I, whose nature is internal intuition (*pratibhā*), desiring to express [the teaching] both in brief and in detail, produce the various wonders of the Siddhāntas and other scriptures. For it is not possible for the body and senses—which are insentient and comparable to clods of earth—to perform such an act; rather, through those various intermediaries, it is I alone who do so.

Regarding the phrase "the creator of all means of valid cognition" (*sarvapramāṇanirmātā*): by this, it is stated that no application of a means of valid cognition is either possible or necessary for the existence of one's own Self as the Great Lord (*svātmamaheśvara*), whose nature is the supreme *Ahaṃtā*. Thus, as the undeniable experiencer of the thought "I am," one's own Self alone is Śiva; He is omnipresent and established from the very beginning within all means of valid cognition. // 47 // 48 // 49 //
Thus, by means of the sequence explained in this way, the yogi—firmly reflecting "all this is my own manifestation"—becomes one whose nature is the Supreme Brahman; so he says:
"In this manner, when the conceptualization of duality has dissolved and the delusive *māyā* has been transcended, one becomes absorbed in Brahman, like water in water or milk in milk. (51)

In this manner, through the practice of reasoning that thoroughly cultivates the realization of "I am everything," when dualistic conceptualization has dissolved and the manifestation of difference has vanished, the knower transcends delusive *māyā*— the non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) consisting of the conceit of self in what is not-self, which is the cause for the manifestation of difference— and having cast off the contraction [of egoity] by means of the realization "I alone am the soul of the universe," he abides in Brahman, which is expansive in nature, full, and a single mass of consciousness-bliss.
Through the dissolution of its contraction, it would merge into its own essential nature (svarūpa) and attain identity with Brahman.
To the question "In what manner?", he says "in water," and so forth.
Just as water drawn up by various jars and the like, or milk mixed with many thousands of cows of diverse breeds such as the Śāvaleyas and Bāhuleyas—[is subsequently unified].

Furthermore, through the complete dissolution of the limitations created by distinctions such as "jar" or "spotted cow," just as water enters water or milk enters milk so that it becomes one and the same substance where no distinction manifests, in the very same way, through the breaking of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) consisting of the body, vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void, one attains Brahman itself. As Bhaṭṭa Divākaravatsa has said:
When the island of bodily perception has dissolved and you have reached the singular, stainless ocean of consciousness,
you shine forth as the eternal, one Self of the universe within, with the entire aggregate of the senses withdrawn and irreversible.
Thus ends the Kakṣyā-stotra, [verse] 51.
Thus, for the yogin who has ascended to the state of Brahman, even the overcoming by dualities is composed of Brahman alone and does not prevail to destroy his true nature; so he says:
"When the collection of principles has thus attained the state of being Śiva through meditation, what grief and what delusion can there be for one who perceives everything as Brahman? (52)

In this manner, for the yogin whose bonds of the sheath have dissolved, through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) upon the collection of principles— the aggregate of the elements, objects, and senses—

and by means of a firm realization that "all this is one's own self-consciousness," the state of being Śiva is attained; having reached the nature of supreme non-duality, for him who perceives this entire multitude of principles as Brahman, there is no longer any oppression by the pairs of opposites characterized by grief and delusion.
Since they are all composed of Brahman and are thus identical with their own true nature, none of them at all have the power to cause distress. // 52 //

One might object: "Even for a knower whose nature is supreme non-duality, why should there not necessarily be an accumulation of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma caused by that [body] while the body still persists? To this he provides the answer:
"The fruit of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, arises only from association with false knowledge;
for the fault of association is as harmful to one who is not a thief as the contact of a weapon is to one who is not a thief. (53)

Even the accumulation of a heap of results from meritorious and non-meritorious actions, such as the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) or the killing of a Brahmin, arises solely from association with false knowledge. That is to say, through that perverse knowledge characterized by the conceit of self in what is not-self—such as "I am the body" or "let this horse-sacrifice and so forth be my means"—there arises an attachment; it is precisely from that [attachment] that the animal (the bound soul) accumulates the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious karma.
By that [association], one becomes a vessel for the afflictions of saṃsāra, being incessantly permeated by them.

Now, one might ask: "Even for a cognizer whose nature is Brahman, how does such a thing result in the state of a bound soul (paśutva)? To this, he introduces another point with the words "For it is unequal," and so forth.
Because the fault of association is entirely intolerable; just as contact with the wicked results in the transfer of one's own faults even to one who is extremely virtuous.

In the same way, even for a pure subject, the association with delusion born of non-recognition (akhyāti) brings about the state of a bound soul (paśutva) and bestows the connection with auspicious and inauspicious karma. // 53 //
Even birth, death, and so forth do not belong to the yogin who has realized the nature of Brahman, but rather only to those subjects under the influence of *māyā*; thus he says:
"The deluded ones here who worship ignorance, which creates worldly conventions—they go through birth and death, bound by the bolts of merit and demerit. (54)

Those knowers who, identifying the body as the self and being defiled by the desire for fruits, resort in this world to that ignorance consisting of merit and demerit which takes the form of worldly custom— that *māyā* whose nature is the manifestation of duality— as a means for attaining results such as heaven and hell;
they are deluded and ignorant, bound by the shackles of merit and demerit, and are born again and again and die for the sake of experiencing those very fruits.

Thus, they become partakers of the incessant afflictions of saṃsāra; however, the yogin—whose veil of delusion is utterly destroyed, whose bondage of dharma and adharma has dissolved, and whose nature is Brahman—is neither born nor does he die. // 54 //
Thus, he says that even those karmas acquired through ignorance are destroyed only by the manifestation of knowledge, and not otherwise:
"But karma, consisting of merit and demerit, accumulated during the time of ignorance, perishes through the power of the light of higher knowledge, just like cotton long stored away. (55)

That which was accumulated and accepted as action consisting of merit and demerit during the time of ignorance—the occasion of the conceit of being a false subject—is destroyed by the power of the light of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*), that is, by the power of the light of specific knowledge. This "light" is the radiance arising from the repeated reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*) of that higher knowledge which is capable of burning away the false state of being a subject, [namely] the realization: "I am indeed the Supreme Brahman."
By its power, that [accumulation] goes to non-appearance.

To what is it like? He says: "Like cotton long accumulated. Just as cotton or swan-down, long accumulated, is instantly reduced to ashes by the force of a blazing fire, even so the entire mass of the fruits of karma is, in the midst of a single moment, [reduced to nothing] by the power of the fire of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It goes to dissolution. As it is said in the Gītā: "Just as a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes."
Thus [ends verse] 55.

Not only does past karma dissolve through the clarity of knowledge, but even present karma, when viewed with a vision kindled by knowledge, does not culminate in the experience of its fruit. Thus he says:
"Upon the attainment of knowledge, even that which has been performed does not lead to fruit; therefore, how could there be rebirth for him?
Having transcended the bond of previous births, he shines as the sun of Śiva with his own rays. (56)

When the reflective awareness of oneself as the Great Lord (Maheśvara) has taken root, even karma—whether auspicious, inauspicious, or otherwise—is rendered incapable of yielding its corresponding fruit due to the absence of the conceit of being a conditioned subject (*kṛtrima-pramātṛtā*). Consequently, because of the absence of the fruits of karma, by what means could there be the existence of a birth suitable for experiencing them?
The meaning is that for the yogin, there is no rebirth.

If it is asked, "If he is not born again from that alms-food, then what would he be like? the author says, "one whose birth has passed," and so forth. He is thus one for whom the connection—that is, the bond—of the form of birth has passed away; with his own rays, which are a mass of the light of consciousness, he shines and radiates as the sun in the form of Śiva, and is not [merely] as imagined by other philosophical systems.

Liberation for this [individual] is not the attainment of something elsewhere; rather, it is simply the attainment of the expansion of one's own powers through the destruction of the contraction produced by the coverings (kañcukas) such as Māyā. // 56 //
Regarding this very point, he states the reasoning:

"Just as a seed freed from its husk, chaff, and awn produces a sprout, so too the Self, when liberated from the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* bonds, does not produce the sprout of worldly existence. (57)

Just as a rice seed, when separated from its awn, husk, and chaff, does not become the cause for the effect characterized by the production of a sprout— even while situated amidst earth, water, and sunlight— due to the absence of the causal complex consisting of the awn and so forth which constitute its nature as a seed; in exactly the same way, [the self] is liberated and becomes distinct when freed from the *āṇava* impurity, which stands in the place of the chaff, the *māyīya* impurity, which stands in the place of the husk, and the *kārmika* impurity, which stands in the place of the awn.

The Self, being consciousness, does not produce the sprout of existence—the growth of saṃsāra—due to the absence of the causal complex consisting of the three impurities; rather, it is Maheśvara alone who, while intuitively perceiving within Himself the manifold variety of the appearance and disappearance of the multitude of diverse objects pervading the universe, exists as such. // 57 //

Thus, for the knower whose seed-skin has been burnt by the fire of knowledge, there is no ground for any doubt regarding what is to be abandoned or what is to be accepted; therefore, he says: "The knower of the Self fears nothing whatsoever, for everything is his own essential nature.
And he does not grieve at all, because in the ultimate sense, there is no destruction. (58)

He who knows the Self—that is, he who knows the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of his own Great Lord (Maheśvara)—fears nothing whatsoever; he does not take up fear from any king, enemy, or living beings. Why is this so? He says: "For everything is his own innate form. Because for him—who knows the non-duality of his own Self as the Great Lord—all this multitude of objects, this entire universe, is the form and appearance of his own innate Self, whose sole body is the Great Light.

"Because light pervades everything"—thus, by its own sovereignty, light itself shines as both self and other. For this very reason, whatever appears in the world as an object of fear is, for that [consciousness], just like its own limb; how could it produce fear, since an entity distinct from one's own self would have to be the cause of fear? Furthermore, what could possibly serve as a limit for that which is completely full on all sides?

Since there exists a distinct state beginning with fear and so forth— such that even a knower (*jñānin*), though having cast aside the conceit of identifying the body as the self, might still be afraid— it follows that because one’s own true nature is perceived everywhere,
one who stands within *saṃsāra* moves about entirely free from doubt, being alone and having dissolved the distinction between self and other.
As it was said by the venerable Parameṣṭhin:
O Lord, for one who perceives this entire mandala of objects as non-conceptual and as Your very body,
when the world is filled by nothing but one's own self, whence can there be fear for that eternally blissful person?
Thus [it is said]. The author also says:
"In this cycle of existence, a person suffers from the passion for fear and daring, thinking, 'I am alone.
But when one thinks, 'I am alone,' who else is there that belongs to me? Thus I remain established, free from fear."
Thus [it is said], and furthermore: "He does not grieve," and so forth.

Nor does the knower of the Self grieve as one might over the loss of wealth, wife, and the like, thinking, "I am destitute," "I am overcome by disease," or "I am dying," because, according to the sequence already explained, he is inward-turned toward the ultimate, real entity which is of the nature of consciousness.
Perishability and the nature of decay do not exist in the mere subject (*pramātṛ*).
For everything that appears as an effect, whose essence consists of objective representation (*abhimāna*) and which is delimited by "this-ness" (*idantā*), arises and perishes;

but this is not the case for the Self, which consists of consciousness, whose essence is "I-ness" (*ahantā*), which is uncreated and autonomous, since no effort directed toward an effect is perceived in it.

And for the yogin who reflects that "the essential nature [of the Self] would not suffer destruction by this much," there will be no manifestation of grief and the like caused by that [body], even while remaining in the body, because such manifestations do not obscure the essential nature. // 58 //

Furthermore, he demonstrates that by virtue of the firmness gained from the constant cultivation of the nature of one’s own Self as the Great Lord (Maheśvara), no defect such as incompleteness can arise in the mind of this Knower:

"For one who possesses a mass of jewels of ultimate reality grown within the treasury of the most secret heart, what misfortune could there be, and for whom, when abiding in the state of the Great Lord, thinking 'I am indeed [He]'? (59)

The "extremely hidden" (*atigūḍha*) treasury is the heart itself, which by its very nature is a storehouse where one rests in the true essence of all ultimate reality. Within that [heart] is the ultimate truth—the true nature of self-knowledge as taught by the authentic Guru—which has taken root through the most intense and profound confidence. Because it is the cause of all manifestations, it is like a "collection of jewels" (*ratnasaṃcaya*). For that reason, [one realizes]: "I alone am all this."

When that state of Maheśvara— which has manifested as full and is characterized by repose in supreme I-consciousness— exists as the freedom of the self-luminous nature of one's own Self even for an embodied being, what indeed could be a wretched misfortune, a state of poverty, or any artificial excellence such as prosperity and the like, which is merely indicated by those conditions?

Since all objects have appearance as their essence, at the very moment they appear, the yogin—being identical with his own Self—is how could he be subject to superiority or inferiority? Thus, no such thing as misfortune can exist. For whom, then, or what indeed would be the locus of this misfortune? Indeed, those who identify the body and so forth as the Self would be the locus of this misfortune, because they are masters over the attainment of an object of desire distinct from themselves, yet become destitute when that is taken away.

Thus, how could that Knower—who is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) because he possesses the ultimate realization of non-artificial *ahantā* and thinks "I am everything" through an inseparable object of desire—be a vessel for wretchedness and the like? For such a state is impossible due to the absence of any attainment or non-attainment of something external. Therefore...

The epithets "treasury" (*gañja*), "accumulation of jewels" (*ratnasaṃcaya*), and "lord" (*īśvara*) have been established as designating the Great One (*mahat*)—the unconditioned ultimate reality that has taken root in the heart. (59)
Now he describes the nature of liberation:
"Liberation has no abode whatsoever, nor is there any going elsewhere;
liberation is the breaking of the knot of ignorance and the manifestation of one's own power. (60)

There exists no separate abode or location for liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the absolute I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*) whose essence is the wonder of the Self and which is *kaivalya* (isolation), because it is devoid of limitations by space, time, or form. For this very reason, there is no going elsewhere to a distinct place;

liberation is not a dissolution (*laya*) as it is conceived in the view of dualists, who maintain that through the process of departure (*utkrānti*), one pierces the centers of the body (*cakrādhāra*, etc. and dissolves upward into the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).
"This alone is liberation. As it has been said:
"What is the purpose of departing [from the body] when Śiva-nature is all-pervasive?
For what purpose is there a departure when the supreme reality is non-pervasive?"

Thus, there are many other such varieties of liberation imagined by other schools; however, as they would lead to an excessive lengthening of this work, they are not elaborated upon here. Since the stain of duality is present everywhere, the desire for liberation in what is actually non-liberation is merely a semblance of liberation.
Furthermore, he states "ignorance," and so forth, to explain what the characteristic of liberation is.

Ignorance is delusion (*moha*), characterized by the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) with respect to the non-self, such as the body and so on, preceded by the conceit of non-self with respect to the Self; this arises from non-manifestation (*akhyāti*). Because it causes the contraction of one's full essential nature, it is like a knot (*granthi*). [It is the knot] of that which is characterized by one's own sovereignty (*svātantrya*).

Bondage consists in the identification with the body and so forth regarding one's own pervasiveness and other qualities; its "piercing" (*bhitt*) is the breaking of that [bondage], which is the tearing asunder of the knot characterized by identification with the body and so forth through the firmness of cultivating one's own full self-nature and autonomy.

By means of that cause—namely, through one's own powers (*svaśaktibhiḥ*), which are attributes characterized by the autonomy of one's own self—the state of manifestation is the blossoming of the powers of one's own self. This alone is unsurpassed liberation.

This is the intended meaning: just as space, though endowed with qualities such as being innate, eternal, and all-pervasive, is called "the space within a jar" when it is contracted by the confinement of walls such as a jar—

and thus appears as if distinct from space itself, being characterized by qualities such as non-pervasiveness— it nevertheless becomes endowed once again, at that very moment, with qualities such as pervasiveness upon the dissolution of the contraction caused by the walls of the jar and so forth.
It may be that no new property whatsoever arises from the destruction of a jar or similar object;

likewise, consciousness (caitanya), when contracted by the limitation produced through identification with the body and so forth, is said to be as if bound. That very same consciousness, however, through the manifestation of knowledge of its own true nature and the dissolution of the bondage of being a limited subject (pramātṛtā) relative to the body and so forth, blossoms through the discernment of its own powers.

Bondage and liberation, which consist merely of the conceit "as if liberated," exist only in relation to a limited subject; however, in the ultimate sense, nothing whatsoever occurs within the reality of consciousness itself.
Therefore, in liberation, nothing new is accomplished; rather, one's own innate nature simply manifests.
This very point is also stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
"Just as by the construction of a well, the space within the water is not created [as something new], but that which already exists is merely brought into manifestation;
for how could there be the arising of what is non-existent?"
Just as when a leather bag is burst, the air within is not distinct from the surrounding air,
so too the self, once its bonds of merit and demerit are exhausted, is not separate from Brahman.
Thus [ends verse] 60.

Thus, one whose bond of ignorance has been destroyed, even while maintaining a body for the sake of favoring others, is liberated; this is declared as follows: "One whose knot of ignorance is severed, whose doubt has vanished, whose delusion is dispelled, and whose merit and sin are exhausted—he is liberated even while joined with a physical frame. (61)

Even while connected with a body, because he lacks the conceit (*abhimāna*) of identifying with the body and so forth due to the expansion of his knowledge of his own Self, he is liberated even while living and becomes one whose power is fully blossomed. Now, [an objection is raised]: "Is not the very union with a physical form (*vigraha*) bondage? How can he be liberated while still connected to it? To this, he says "bhinna" and so forth: "He by whom the knot consisting of ignorance—which arises from the manifestation of incompleteness and takes the form of the conceit of body and so forth—has been split asunder or torn open; he is thus [described]."

"Thus, with doubts gone" means for this very reason his uncertainty has perished. "By whom delusion is cast aside" means he by whom the error consisting of duality—the delusion—is rejected or surpassed through the attainment of supreme non-dual knowledge (*paramādvayajñāna*). One of such a kind is he whose merits and demerits have been exhausted through such constant cultivation, whose latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) have dissolved, and for whom there is an absence of the conceit that the body is the self, [and thus] whose virtues and non-virtues have vanished.
By this, it is established that ignorance alone is bondage.

And for one in whom that [ignorance] has been destroyed even while in union with a body, he is liberated at that very moment while still living; it is not the case, however, that union with the body is bondage and its departure is liberation, but rather that full liberation occurs only upon the fall of the body. // 61 //

Even while the body—the cause of action—remains for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the action performed merely for the sake of maintaining the bodily journey does not lead to fruit for him, because it is kindled by knowledge. He states the reasoning for this:
"Just as a seed scorched by fire becomes incapable of sprouting, so too action, when scorched by the fire of knowledge, does not grant rebirth. (62)

Just as a grain of rice scorched by fire becomes incapable of producing a sprout or the like, even when situated amidst the collection of conditions such as earth, water, and sunlight due to the deficiency of its causal totality (*sāmagrīvaikalyāt*), in the same way, karma— burnt by the fire of knowledge and consumed by the radiance of supreme non-dual awareness— is rendered powerless. This occurs through the abandonment of the conceit of selfhood regarding the body and so forth, in the form of the realization "I alone thus manifest as the soul of the universe," and through the relinquishing of the intellect that discriminates between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.

Whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed, its potency is burnt away; it does not again yield the fruit of birth for the Knower immediately after the consumption of alms-food. It fails to become a cause for the formation of a body, just as a burnt seed cannot produce a sprout.

Therefore, because the power of consciousness—which consists of the sense of "I" in its entirety—has no further attachment to results, an action performed [by one who has realized this] is not capable of granting another birth. // 62 //
Furthermore, he explains how the consciousness-power (*citiśakti*), though thus blossoming, can become embodied:

"For, through the limited nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and by means of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding a future body appropriate for its karma, consciousness becomes contracted; upon the destruction of this body, it shines forth in that [new] way. (63)

Because, due to limited intellect—which is born of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)—and a determination clouded by desire preceded by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of identifying with the body and so forth, one performs an action characterized by such latent impressions, thinking: "I shall sacrifice with a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); may I be happy here and in the hereafter; may I never be miserable; through this action, may I attain the status of Indra. It is for one thus distinguished by latent impressions [that the following applies].

Thus, for the agent, action is favorable; that future body— which is suitable for experiencing results corresponding to that action whose growth has been attained through mental latent impressions (vāsanā), and which will come into being subsequently upon the exhaustion of the authority over the body that experiences the fruits of *prārabdha* karma—

is [shaped] by that very latent impression (*bhāvanā*), namely, the ascension of the desire for the fruit of a desired action, such as "May I attain sovereignty through this horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites."

Through the cultivation of a future body appropriate to its karma, this power of consciousness (citiśakti), though entirely full, becomes permeated by the impurity of action (kārmamala) rooted in the impurities of finitude (āṇava) and illusion (māyīya); consequently, although all-pervasive, it becomes contracted—like the space within a jar—and comes to possess limitations consisting of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of a body that experiences results in accordance with its karma.
Thus, upon the destruction of this [present] body, it becomes [a new one] in that same manner.
When there is the destruction of that body which is the experiencer of the fruit of this commenced karma—
destruction meaning death— then that consciousness (citi), possessing the latent impressions (vāsanā) of karma that have arisen,

becomes such that it possesses a body as the experiencer of the fruit of that karma by which the previous karmic fruit was acquired; it is by virtue of this that the consciousness also [assumes such a state].
It would become a vessel for experiencing the fruits of heaven, hell, and so forth.

Therefore, having become embodied, whatever action is performed out of a craving for limited results has the power to inevitably grant a birth as an enjoyer of those fruits. However, that which is performed while not being embodied—by way of the nature of pure consciousness, with the realization "I am all Brahman"—cannot lead to birth, because it does not provide the soil for the sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the essential meaning.

If it is argued that, being thus devoid of selfhood (*anātmatā*), action accumulated [by the subject] leads to transmigration, then the true nature of the Self must be explained so that one would no longer be a transmigrator; therefore, although this has already been established, he speaks again in order to make it penetrate the hearts of his disciples:
"But if [one realizes] stainless consciousness (*bodha*), which consists of a cognizer and agent who has transcended all [limitations]..."
His form is light, with the mind expanded and free from rising or setting; his resolve is true. // 64 //
The Lord is devoid of spatial and temporal divisions, eternal, immutable, and perfectly complete;
He alone is the sole agent who fashions the dissolution and emergence of the vast multitude of powers. // 65 //
One should realize oneself as identical with Śiva, the supreme ordainer of the process of creation and so forth;
how then could one be a transmigrating being? For one who is all-pervading, whence or whither could there be any wandering?

If, however, a cognizer whose heart has been pierced by the descent of supreme *śakti* should cast aside the conceit of being a limited subject centered on the body and so forth, and awaken to his own self as consisting of Śiva—recognizing it as a single mass of consciousness and bliss—then, having fully realized the state of his own self as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), how indeed, and in what manner, could he be a transmigrator, characterized by the tendency to wander? He would not be so; for [his nature] consists of the eightfold subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) which is both conscious and unconscious.

The essential point is this: how can that which is of the nature of Śiva, whose sole form is consciousness, and whose coverings of impurity such as *āṇava* have been destroyed, transmigrate through connection with the impurity of karma (*kārmamala*)?
Having raised the objection—"But what fault would there be if that whose sole form is consciousness were also a transmigrating being?"—he says "vitata" and so forth.

For that cognizer who is expanded—whose space, time, and form are undivided—who is full due to the exhaustion of the latent impressions (vāsanā) previously created by the conceit of being a body and so forth, whence could there be wandering? Since he is all-pervasive, what object exists apart from him such that, in relation to it, he might become detached and perform a movement or transition elsewhere into something distinct? For it is only for one who is delimited by the conceit of being a cognizer limited to a body and so forth that the existence of grammatical factors (kāraka), such as the point of departure (apādāna) and the locus (adhikaraṇa), is possible.

Furthermore, for that cognizer who is a single mass of consciousness, who has become Brahman, and for whom space and time are undivided, there could not even be a verbal formulation regarding transmigratory existence (*saṃsaraṇa*).
To explain what kind of Śiva-nature one should awaken to as the Self, he says: "pure awareness," and so forth.
