That from which the accumulation of impurities such as *āṇava* and the rest has departed—that very [awareness], due to its stainlessness, is "awareness," meaning pure consciousness.

Likewise, he is one whose nature is sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) consisting of knowledge and action, which has transcended all things and is unsurpassed; he is "extended" (*vitata*), meaning pervasive because there is no division caused by space and so forth. Furthermore, he is one whose form or body is that very light (*bhās*)—the radiance of consciousness—in which setting and rising, dissolution and emergence, do not exist. Moreover, he is such that his intentions (*saṃkalpa*) are true in the ultimate sense, being the free exercise of his own will; whatever he desires happens exactly in that way. Such is he.

Likewise, it is devoid of conceptualizations regarding space, time, and form; because it possesses the qualities of pervasiveness and eternity, it is therefore constant, immovable, immutable, and indestructible.
Furthermore, it is the Lord (Īśvara), being independent;
and moreover, it is perfectly complete, being utterly free from all desire.

Thereafter, knowing one's own Self as the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is entirely complete with such attributes as being the independent master over the process of the dissolution and arising of the vast and abundant multitudes of potencies—such as those of jars, cloths, and so forth—which originate from the mass of sounds and are presided over by the powers of Brahmā and others; and who is the Creator (Vedhas) highly skilled and proficient in the rules of creation and so on—one becomes a person whose seeds of karma are burnt out, and while performing whatever action whatsoever, does not partake in saṃsāra again; that is to say, one becomes liberated even while living. // 64 //

Thus, demonstrating that even an action performed by a knower—who has realized the nature of his own self and whose desire for the fruits of action has dissolved—does not lead to a result, he states a worldly illustration established by his own experience: "By these arguments it is also established that the action of a knower is not fruitful; for in the world, there is no fruit [of an act] when there is the firm conviction: 'This is not mine, but rather his. (67)

"I alone am the mass of consciousness, autonomous, performing all actions by virtue of being the innermost essence of all subjects; nor am I the agent, for it is the Supreme Lord’s power of autonomy that acts in this manner—what does this have to do with me, whose nature is pure consciousness? Thus [speaks] the one who knows the true nature of his own self, as explained through reasonings and arguments established previously regarding his essential nature.

For the knower of the Self, because the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth is absent in both ways, action—whether already completed or being performed—is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted;

thus, it is not fruitful and is not joined with its fruit. Since, as previously explained, for such a knower there is an absence of artificiality in both respects, where could even a performed action produce a connection with a fruit? Nowhere at all, because the substrate—the nature of the conceit of being a limited subject consisting of the body and so forth—is absent. This is the meaning.

The firm establishment of the knower’s conceit regarding the fruit of an action performed is precisely what constitutes the locus [of bondage]. However, for the wise man, due to the absence of such conceit, the action is exhausted within his very own nature and does not become connected with a fruit.

Now, one might ask: "Is it not from conceit alone that an action is joined with its fruit? Where is this seen to be so? To this he says: "Not even 'this is mine,'" and so forth. This is observed and is not unprecedented; for example, one thinks, "This ritual act such as a sacrifice is not mine," but rather belongs to some other person who possesses a purpose.

Even if an action such as a sacrifice is performed with the thought, "This is for the sacrificer," because there is no sense of ownership over the fruit—due to seeking only its price in this world—that action is not considered to be endowed with a fruit in the next world. For it is according to the principle that "the officiating priests sacrifice" (*yajanti*) while "the sacrificer sacrifices" (*yajate*); thus, the sacrificial rite belongs to the officiating priests who perform it, [not to the one who merely pays].

Even though they have performed sacrificial rites such as the Aśvamedha, it does not belong to us in the slightest; rather, we are merely those who seek a fixed price for the sake of the merit of the initiated and virtuous sacrificer. Here, there is no one at all who is a true patron (*yajamāna*) such that he would partake in the fruit of heaven or other rewards through this ritual act. Because they lack any sense of ownership over the fruits of their actions, the action, even though performed by them, does not truly belong to them.

The sacrificer is indeed joined with its fruit, such as heaven and so forth; for although he does not perform the sacrificial act himself therein, but merely looks toward the work accomplished by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he maintains the firm conviction:

"This sacrificial act, such as the Aśvamedha, is mine; the priests have engaged in the ritual through my wealth; therefore, the fruit such as heaven will certainly accrue to me alone upon the fall of the body. Thus, even though he does not perform it, that [fruit] belongs to him due to the strength of his identification with the fruit of the desired action.
One is joined with the fruit of action;

for this very reason, when the fruit of the action is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used—as in *yajate* (he sacrifices) or *yajamānaḥ* (the sacrificer)—referring to the initiated agent; but when not intended for the agent (*kartranabhiprāya*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*) is used—as in *yajanti yājakāḥ* (the priests sacrifice).

Such is the greatness of the sovereignty of free will (*vikalpasvātantrya*), which is difficult to transcend: that even an action performed by oneself may, due to the absence of the conceit of ownership over its fruit, not be joined with that fruit.

It is not logical that even an action performed by others would become endowed with fruit for oneself through the strength of the conceit "this is mine"; therefore, just like the activity of officiating priests, an action being performed by a yogin does not bear fruit because of the absence of conceit regarding its results. // 67 //
Thus, he says that the knower whose intellect has abandoned the stain of conceptualizing what is to be rejected or accepted in all actions becomes radiant:

"In this way, the awakened one, having burned away all mental constructs by the wind of meditative cultivation, becomes composed of light while offering oblations into the blazing light of the Self. (68)

In this manner, through the method thus explained, that cultivation which consists of the firm establishment of self-reflection (*vimarśa*) within the Self—namely, "I alone am the Great Lord of Consciousness, and I thus manifest at all times and in every way"—is itself the wind as it gradually expands. By means of that [wind], the knower is awakened, just as fire covered by ashes is awakened by the wind; [he realizes: "I am a bound soul (*paśu*) amidst all conceptual constructions."

Bound by the fetters of karma and embodied in a physical form, all such mental constructs as "this son, wife, and so forth are mine," or "by this karma heaven or hell will come to pass," become subordinate to the realization that "I alone am all this. Offering these into the blazing fire of consciousness— the light of the Self— which consists of the essence of the wonder of supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*), he, by entering into the nature of non-conceptual awareness, becomes composed of light.

Through the complete exhaustion of the fuel of conceptualization regarding the object to be burned, the fire of consciousness itself becomes the form of the burner; that is to say, it remains as the single body of the supreme subject alone. // 68 //
Having explained it in this manner, [the author] says how one who is devoted to the practice of the yoga of supreme knowledge passes his time by means of remaining with what remains:
"Eating whatever it may be, clothed in whatever it may be, peaceful, dwelling wherever he may be—he, whose self is the Self of all beings, is liberated. (69)

Eating whatever object fell before him that was suitable for consumption, he marveled at it; yet, being free from the conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted— such as "this is pure" or "this is impure," "this is coarse food" or "this is sweet food"— he gathered whatever came to him effortlessly, without any fixed rule.

"Thus covered by this," and so forth. Whether covered by a rag, a hide, bark, cotton cloth, or the like, or by divine garments, because there is neither excellence nor deficiency in either case, one who seeks the functional purpose of clothing the body neither hates nor praises anything at all.
How is this so? Because he is peaceful, having transcended conceptual constructions such as pleasure and pain;
likewise, because he is a dweller "anywhere whatsoever.
That is to say, in whatever kind of place it may be, he seeks only his own shelter, and not [specific] fields, abodes, sacred fords, and so forth.

Because of its purity, it is to be accepted; nor is it to be avoided because of impurity, such as that of a cremation ground or the dwelling of a dog-cooker (śvapaca). Without effort, it dwells in whatever place happens to come before it, being free from the stain of conceptualizing purity and impurity. "He is liberated"—thus, by continuing in this manner, engaged in acting for the benefit of others and passing his time, he is liberated and becomes Supreme Śiva.
And it has been said: "The gods know him as a brahmin who is covered by whatever [is available], fed by whatever [is available], and sleeps wherever he may be."
Thus it is said; and also in the *Mokṣadharma*:

"I, being pure, practice this Ājagara vow, which consists of food, drink, and edibles whose fruits are not fixed, which is distributed according to rule by place and time, which is pleasing to the heart, and which is not practiced by the miserly."
Thus it is said. To explain how even one acting in this way the knower may liberate himself, he says: "the Self of all beings.

Because that knower is the Self of all beings—having realized that he is the Self of all beings and all beings are his Self—nothing exists as a cause of bondage; rather, everything conduces to his liberation. // 69 //
Nor does merit or demerit arise for one of such a nature who is free from conceit, even while performing some action; thus he says:

"Even if one performs hundreds of thousands of horse-sacrifices or commits hundreds of thousands of murders of Brahmins, the knower of ultimate reality, being stainless, is touched neither by merits nor by sins. (70)

He who thus knows the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), who understands the true nature of his own self as being essentially the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), may— devoid of desire for fruits and free from the conceit of agency— perform, for the sake of play, the countless sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and Aptoryāma, thinking merely, "This is to be done. Or, if he should commit through negligence unenjoined great sins such as killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, or theft, even in both these cases, because he lacks the conceit of "I" and "mine" due to his bodilessness, it is solely the will of the Supreme Lord that acts thus.
He thinks, "What has happened to me? as he yawns; yet that knower is neither touched nor defiled by merits with their auspicious fruits, nor by sins which are inauspicious.
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "Stainless."
Because his *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* impurities (*malas*), which are the causes of transmigratory existence, have departed— that is, been destroyed—
it is thus for the impure subject that there exists the state of identifying with "self" and "mine" through the fragmented perception of the body and so forth;

by virtue of the wretchedness of such identification— thinking "this action of mine is auspicious" or "this is inauspicious"— there occurs the accumulation of merit and demerit, from which arises the accumulation of the fruits of action.
Since the accumulation of impurities caused by the sense of "mine-ness" has vanished for him due to the absence of ego-inflation, how could there be any contact with merit or sin?
As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"He whose state of being is not characterized by egoism, and whose intellect is not stained..."
Even having slain these worlds, he does not slay, nor is he bound.
Thus [ends the verse]. 70.
Reflecting upon the constant conduct of such a knower, he says:
"Free from pride, joy, anger, passion, despondency, fear, greed, and delusion;
devoid of praise and the *vaṣaṭ* call; like one who is dull-witted, he should wander with a mind free from dispute. (71)

Intoxication (*mada*) is the conceit of being the body as the subject; joy (*harṣa*) is the delight from obtaining what was not previously possessed; anger (*kopa*) is wrath; passion (*manmatha*) is the longing for sexual enjoyment; despondency (*viṣāda*) is the state of delusion resulting from separation from the beloved; fear (*bhaya*) is the dread of an enemy or of lions, tigers, and the like; greed (*lobha*) is miserliness; delusion (*moha*) is the sense of "I" and "mine" toward living beings—these [faculties] are the reflections of the latent impressions of the body situated in the middle.

Even those who have entered into the midst [of the ritual], he completely abandons by means of entering into the nature of non-conceptual consciousness as "I am Brahman," thereby reducing them to nothing but the reflective awareness of his own Self.
Likewise, that which has emerged from the hymns and the *vaṣaṭ*-calls— since there is no object of praise distinct from that [Self]— does not belong to him.
Furthermore, there would be no application of hymns and the like, nor recourse to mantras such as *vaṣaṭ* and so forth, because of the absence of distinct deities;
he would wander about like a mere insentient being, his intellect devoid of argumentation.

Due to his state of fullness and lack of desire, he would act like a madman regarding scriptural rites that are established by valid means of knowledge and consist of specific procedures (*itikartavyatā*).

Or rather, regarding the true nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya-satattva*), his intellect is excluded from the deliberation—along with the knowers (*pramātṛ*)—as to whether "this is appropriate" or "this is not"; nor does he require instruction for himself, nor does he set forth an object of knowledge to instruct others. Having become as if subdued, beholding everything as Brahman, he may wander for the sake of play; thus is he described as being like an insentient being (*jaḍa*). // 71 //

Even though the group beginning with pride has been thus avoided, one might ask: "Why is it that even a man of knowledge (*jñānī*), while still possessing a body, is not touched by these [afflictions] as we are? To this he states the reason:
"This group, beginning with pride and exhilaration, arises from the delusion of duality (*vibheda-sammoha*).
How, then, could the awakening to the non-dual Self (*advaitātma-vibodha*) possibly be touched by it? (72)
Immediately following the commentary on the *Kārikās*, this section on "Intoxication" (*mada*) and so forth begins with the words, "Because of the delusion of differentiation.

This delusion of differentiation, which takes the form of "self" and "mine," arises from the perception of incompleteness; from that, for the bound subjects (*paśu-pramātṛs*), there emerges the sense of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted through the error of duality.
On the other hand, he who possesses the supreme non-dual self-awareness—"I am all, I am Brahman"—is a preeminent knower who is like the sky; by means of that [awareness], he [is liberated].

How indeed could the group beginning with intoxication (madādi) touch it, and in what manner could it be made turbid? For distinct objects may sometimes impart their own nature to another distinct object;

but how could the group beginning with intoxication, when perceived as having become Brahman, lead to contradiction for the knower who has likewise become Brahman, since they are of the same kind? // 72 //
Even the section on external praise and oblation is based solely on duality and is not sufficient for his satisfaction; thus he says:
"There is nothing whatsoever separate from him that is to be praised or offered as a sacrifice.
He would be satisfied by praise and the like only when he is liberated, being free from prostrations and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*. (73)

For the knower of reality, whose nature is non-dual awareness, there exists nothing separate or distinct in form that could be praised or offered as a deity or as an oblation; nor does he attain satisfaction through praise and the like performed as something to be done (*kartavya*). This is because, being composed of eternal bliss through the enjoyment of the realization of non-duality, he does not value artificial pleasure. Therefore, he has emerged from [the sphere of] salutations and *vaṣaṭ* offerings.
He who is such is indeed liberated; thus he is praised in the Vedāntas. // 73 //

Furthermore, he has no need for a separate temple; his own body alone is the abode of the deity of the Self, or rather the locus of consciousness, and nothing else whatsoever. Thus, [the author] says that he does not have a separate temple:
"His body, composed of the thirty-six principles, is filled with the windows of its structural arrangement;
or else, his own body, or another such as a jar, is his temple. (74)
For that man of knowledge, his own body or the body of another is indeed the temple of the deity, because it serves as the substratum for the enjoyment of the deity who is one's own Self.

However, an external temple, such as Mount Meru or other palaces, becomes a "house of the gods" only when it has been mentally constructed by the Guru through the pervasion of the body in the form of the arrangement of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*); and if even the deity residing therein is grasped by the practitioner through the pervasion of one's own Self as a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), then [it truly becomes a divine abode].
Otherwise, if that [body] were not a deity there, how could this pair—being inert like a fragment of stone—liberate devotees or lead them to the state of proximity (*sāmīpya*) and so forth?

Thus, in its primary sense, the body is the "temple" (*devagṛha*) because it is the locus of consciousness; for one who is fully awakened, his own Self, which resides within that [body], is the deity for everyone, and thus the body itself is the temple.
To explain what that [temple] is like, he says: "the thirty-six principles" (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*).

The external [temple] is conceived through its pervasion by the thirty-six principles; however, the supreme temple of the body (*dehadevagṛha*) is, moreover, directly filled and nourished by the thirty-six principles. While there is the arrangement of windows in an external temple, this [body-temple], on the other hand, is completely filled with windows consisting of the arrangement of the limbs (*vigraha*); thus it is said "in the body."

The arrangement within the body—the sequential order of the doors of the senses—is itself the conceptualization of the temple; because it is filled by that [consciousness] and remains unimpaired, it is like an external temple.
Not only is the body the abode of consciousness and thus a temple, but he says "or even a jar and so forth" to indicate that whatever is presided over by consciousness is all its temple.

This pentad of objects, characterized by jars and the like, which exists as the nature of the enjoyed, is presided over by consciousness through the gates of the eyes and other senses; thus, according to the teaching of the *Spanda-śāstra*, the Knower himself always abides everywhere in the form of the enjoyed. Therefore, from the perspective of one who possesses knowledge, the entire universe—jars and so forth—is composed of consciousness alone, being a "body of existence" (*bhāva-śarīra*), just like the body of the elements.

Having made even that [the universe] non-different from himself, like his own body, he regards the temple as the house of the Lord—the playful, independent Great Lord who is one's own Self—and as the substratum for his enjoyment. // 74 //

It is said that while a devotee is seen intent on worshipping a deity in an external temple after first bringing flowers and other offerings, what does the Knower do when presiding over the body as a temple? To this he says:
And there, he remains worshipping with the pure substances of self-reflection the deity Paramātman Mahābhairava Śiva, together with his own Śakti. (75)
In that temple of his own body, the supreme and most excellent yogin—who is the Self characterized by consciousness—dwells perpetually worshipping the deity Śiva, who is none other than Bhairava.

He is called Bhairava because he is capable of dissolving all objects of experience, such as sound and the rest; his nature consists of *bharaṇa* (sustaining), *ravaṇa* (shouting), and *vamana* (vomiting).
That very deity is Śiva, whose form is the highest auspiciousness. He remains worshipping her incessantly, in the manner that will be described hereafter.
Satisfying her in due order, one should cause her to radiate.

Now, since an external deity is accompanied by a retinue, with what kind of retinue should one worship her? To this he says: "accompanied by her own powers" (*svaśaktiyutām*). Her own powers are the capacities of the senses, such as sight and so forth, which consist of the manifestations of the powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action—powers that are of the nature of rays of consciousness. Accompanied by these, she is completely surrounded.
To the question "With what does he remain performing worship?", he says: "The self-reflection," and so forth.

This "self-reflection" (*āmarśana*)—the realization that "all this is indeed one's own Self"—is that supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by resting in the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) through the nature of consciousness of all objects.
By means of that, because the stain of the impurity of duality is completely destroyed, there are those [objects] which are pure, consisting of the fivefold objects such as sound and the rest.

"For the sake of worship, substances purified by the removal of dullness—by means of those pure substances which consist of self-reflection. This is the intended meaning: the Knower, having abandoned the stain of the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, gathers the five objects such as sound that present themselves effortlessly through the goddesses of the senses, such as hearing; then, experiencing wonder within himself, he brings them into non-difference with his own Self, thus continuously.

The experts in the secret doctrine maintain that at the time of perceiving each sense-object, the wonder that arises through internal differentiation—the flashing forth of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness)—is itself the worship of one’s own self as the deity.

Therefore, for one who possesses focused attention, at every moment during the apprehension of objects such as sound and the rest, one should become a worshiper of one’s own self as the deity; thus, these very objects like sound are the implements of worship.
Rājānaka Rāma has composed this very point by way of praise:

"In that You are satisfied by Your powers, such as Taijasī and the others, who are busily engaged in offering the world's existence as a sacrifice, which is brought forth by their eternally unrestrained and intense exertion."
In this body, which is a dwelling place for the cemetery and a mass of flesh, blood, fat, and bones, show your terrifying form to me, a hero wandering through the night of worldly existence.
Thus [ends verse] 75.
Thinking that at the conclusion of the worship there ought to be an oblation into the fire, the Knower explains how that is so:

"For one who offers the entire mass of seeds of differentiation consisting of external and internal mental constructs, the oblation occurs effortlessly in the intensely blazing fire of pure consciousness. (76)

For such a person, who is a worshiper of his own self as the deity, there occurs a *homa*—an offering that satisfies the fire—spontaneously, without effort, in the intensely blazing fire of consciousness which shines with the wonder of supreme *ahantā*, even without the hardship of taking up sesame seeds, clarified butter, fuel, and so forth.
To the question "Doing what?", he says: "Externally and internally," and so on.

The differentiation between the external object of cognition, such as blue and so forth, and the internal conceptualization regarding the subject— whether self or other— as well as the conceptualization regarding the internal objects of apprehension, such as pleasure and so forth; this very differentiation between the external and internal subject and object, whose nature consists in the functions of determination, conceptualization, and conceit, is itself the "great seed," because from it arises that [subject-object duality] which takes the form of conceptual construction.

The "accumulation" refers to the collection of that which constitutes the seed of duality; because duality is infinite, it is a "heap. For one who offers this heap by means of the vision of supreme non-duality—that is, by entering the nature of non-conceptualizing consciousness—while sacrificing it into the fire of one's own Self, this is the intended meaning: for the yogi whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, the natural cessation of the conceptualization of self, other, subject, and object, arising from the absence of the conceit of being a limited subject such as the body, is itself the unartificial *homa*.
As the venerable Bhaṭṭa Vīravāmana said:
"In that sacrifice where the fuel is the forest of duality and death itself is the great victim,
we worship eternally with that extraordinary sacrifice."
Thus [ends verse] 76.
Regarding the meditation of such a sacrificer, he says:
"Furthermore, this Blessed One creates various forms through meditation that never sets;
that very meditation is the state of having a true form inscribed by volition. (77)

There is a cessation of the form contemplated with a fixed shape due to the movement of the mental activity elsewhere; however, this meditation is undiminished because this Blessed One, the infinite Maheśvara whose nature is his own self, through the sovereignty of conceptualization which is the very essence of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*),
incessantly creates various forms— objects of diverse kinds in the form of conceptualizations— within the mirror of the intellect.
One contemplates that very same [reality], which is devoid of rising and setting; this is his meditation and reflection, and nothing other than this.
In other cases, however, regarding a specific deity, there would be a restriction based on the conceptualization of various faces and limbs.

But for one who knows that every mental activity is a sprout-like manifestation of the expansion of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), all of this is incessantly become the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*).
Likewise, that meditation whose true nature and ultimate reality consist of what is drawn by the mental faculty of volition and depicted upon the wall of consciousness;

for in this way, all this which appears—though it is delineated by conceptual construction and consists of the activity of the mind—is true, because it is not distinct from the Light of consciousness, since consciousness permeates everything.
Thus it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda-śāstra*:
Wherever the mind goes, one should fix it right there;
for even if it wanders, where can it go, since everything is composed of Śiva?
Thus it is said in the Śaivopaniṣad:
"O Beloved, wherever the mind goes—whether externally or internally—therein lies the state of Śiva; because of its all-pervasiveness, where could it go?"
Thus, for this reason, this meditation of the yogin arises spontaneously. // 77 //
Regarding what his recitation (*japa*) should be like, he says:

"That which causes the entire series of worlds, the conceptualization of the sequence of the principles (*tattva*), and the group of sense organs to revolve within internal consciousness—that is declared to be his recitation. (78)

That reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of the universe as non-different from the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*), occurring at every moment according to the sequence to be described, is declared to be its "recitation" (*japa*); it is said to be unartificial.

To the question "What is that?", he says: "The entire series of worlds"—that is, the complete row of enclosures numbering two hundred and twenty-four, which exist within the aggregate of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*s)—as well as "the conceptualization of the sequence of the principles," namely the sequence of the principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.

He causes conceptualization (*parikalpanā*), discernment (*pariccheda*), and the group of sense organs (*akṣagaṇa*)—meaning the collection of faculties consisting of the internal and external instruments—to revolve within internal consciousness (*antarbodha*). This consciousness is one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), which serves as the central thread for the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*). He causes this revolution through the sequence of the flow of *nāda* and *bindu*, like a waterwheel (*araghaṭṭa-ghaṭīyantra*), according to the sequence of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal (*sṛṣṭi-sthiti-saṃhāra*) occurring with every impulse of the vital breath.

This means that [the practitioner] causes all of this to revolve within his own self-awareness, reflecting upon it at every moment by way of the *nāda* (the primordial sound). This very state, characterized by resting in the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), is his unartificial recitation (*japa*).

The underlying intention is as follows: recitation is indeed the utterance of a mantra—the signifier—of a deity who exists in the form of the signified; and that [utterance] is to be counted by means of a rosary through the sequence of turning the beads, which is pervaded by the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*).

For the supreme non-dual yogi, however, his own vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*), which serves as the thread, flows through the central breath (*madhyama-prāṇa*) in a continuous succession; arising spontaneously by its own nature, it perceives the senses while encompassing them all. Since this entire universe of thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva*), consisting of the denotable (*vācya*), is established within the vital power alone, it is of the nature of the Supreme (*parā-svabhāva*) through the process of rising and subsiding in accordance with every pulsation of the breath.
The Blessed Lady, having taken recourse to the nature of the vital breath and reflecting upon every pulsation of the breath, accomplishes the unartificial recitation (*japa*) for the attentive yogin.
Here, the count of the recitation is twenty-one thousand six hundred times during the day and night.
The recitation of the Goddess has been described as easy to perform, yet difficult for the dull-witted to achieve.
Thus it is said in the Śaiva Upaniṣad;
in the Śivasūtras, [it is stated that] the recitation of the narrative is *japa*.
Thus, this [truth] is the domain only of those whose feet are worthy of worship and who possess attentive concentration. // 78 //
"This is his vow," he says;

for by means of the vision of the universal pledge (*samaya*), whatever he sees and whatever consciousness he conceives is perceived as being intent upon the cremation ground of the universe, fashioned with the conceptualization of the body as a *khaṭvāṅga* staff. (79)

That he holds in his own hand a skull-cup, the vessel of experience, filled with the essence-liquor of the universe, and that he partakes of it—this is his vow, which is both extremely difficult to attain and easily attained. (80)

Thus, that which is about to be described is precisely this vow (*vrata*)—the discipline (*niyama*) for the worship of one's own self as the deity—of this man of knowledge (*jñānin*). As to what kind it is, he says: "both very difficult to attain and easy to attain. It is very difficult to attain because it requires great effort in the form of abandoning other means through the exhaustion of ignorance (*akhyāti*); yet it is easy to attain through the grace of the Supreme Lord.

It is "very difficult to obtain" because it is obtained from this [source]; yet it is also "easy to obtain" because it is obtained with ease, without the torment of adopting external ornaments such as bones and ashes, or restrictive dietary rules and the like.
To the question "What is that vow?", he says: "All," and so forth.

That which is this entire world of conventional appearance, manifesting in the form of diversity, is perceived through the vision of non-duality—by means of the cultivation of reasoning, scripture, and experience—as "I alone shine as all this.
As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self..."
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives with equal vision everywhere.
And so forth. Thus, the very firmness of the cognition of non-duality is itself the *vrata*.
Furthermore, that which one regards as consciousness (*saṃvit*)—which is intent upon the cremation ground of the universe—is also the *vrata*.

For example, [regarding] the universe as having the nature of the grasped and the grasper, and as being overrun by hundreds of corpses in the form of insentient objects such as jars, bodies, and the like.

Having made that very cremation ground—the *pitṛvana*—because from it arises the one, non-inert, Blessed Consciousness (*saṃvid*), and because everything else manifested by Her is like a corpse, being inert; therefore, there is a resemblance between the universe and a cremation ground.

In that universal cremation ground, which is utterly terrifying due to its nature as both birth and death, he considers—that is, he realizes—that Consciousness remains in the center, entirely delighted.

Indeed, this practitioner dwells in the cremation ground; moreover, he is an extraordinary practitioner who, thinking "I alone am the ultimate reality of the single principle of consciousness everywhere," engages like a madman in play with the inert subjects— beasts— and with objects of cognition such as jars, which are like the dead, while occupying this realm of transmigratory existence whose nature is that of a cremation ground, terrifying because it is the site of the dissolution of all subjects and objects.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he who considers consciousness to be fashioned by the conceptualization of the body as a *khaṭvāṅga*":

the *vigraha* is the body; that very thing is the conceptualization of a *khaṭvāṅga*, a ritual arrangement of a skeleton. For the yogi—who, due to the destruction of the stubborn grasping of the conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) within his own body, considers his own self to be transcendent of the body—the body has become a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). He determines that his own body is essentially nothing more than a corpse.

The "skeleton-seal" (kaṅkālamudrā) refers to that [body] which is fashioned as such and sealed as the substratum of experience. For one who observes the hero-vow (vīravratī) while staying in a cremation ground, he must be characterized by the "skull-topped staff seal" (khaṭvāṅgamudrā). Therefore, even for this person whose body is his own self-awareness, since he perceives even his own body as distinct due to its being an object of cognition, that very [awareness] is the skull-topped staff seal; this too is his vow.

Likewise, it tastes—that is, it chews—the "fragmentary potsherd" (*vedyakhaṇḍakakapāla*). This "knowable" (*vedya*)—characterized by the fivefold objects such as sound and so forth, consisting of all that is to be enjoyed—is a "fragment" (*khaṇḍaka*) because it is delimited by its status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and an effect (*kāryatva*);

it is like a shard (*karpara*), a mere fragment of a skull (*kapāla*), specifically a piece of bone from the head. That very thing it "tastes" by means of extracting its essence through the process of resting in full *ahaṃtā*.
"Marvel!"—this too is a vow.
Indeed, the practitioner of the vow (vratin) relishes the "hero's drink" (vīrapāna) contained within the skull; thus he says, "the essence of the universe" (viśvarasa).

Within the skull-fragment consisting of the fivefold objects of perception—namely sound and the rest—that which is the essential portion, the part composed of the nectar of aesthetic savor (carvaṇāmṛta), that alone is the "essence of the juices" (rasāsava), the supreme drink, because it bestows supreme bliss.
"Filled with that" means completely brimming.

This is what is meant: that which is the hard portion of the universe, comparable to a wooden splinter and serving as a vessel, is the skull-cup (*kapāla*); the essential part contained within it, which is capable of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) because it bestows delight, is the "drink" (*pāna*).
Thus, he says "held in his own hand" (*nijakaraga*) to indicate that the skull-cup is in the possession of the practitioner (*vratin*).

One's own rays (*nijakarāḥ*)—which are the rays of consciousness whose nature is the goddesses of the instruments such as the eyes—become objects (*viṣayatva*) as fragments of that which is to be known (*vedyakhaṇḍaka*) by way of being enjoyed.

Thus, it is "held in one's own hands" (*nijakaraga*); just as a drink is drunk with a skull-cup held in the hand, in the very same way, the yogi, having gathered the wine of the essence of the universe (*viśvarasāsava*) with the hand-like perceptions of the eyes and other senses, tastes it by means of the skull-cup of the fragment of the object of knowledge.

This is the intention of the yogi: always bringing the fivefold objects of sense as they arise through the goddesses of the senses, he resorts by means of yoga to an uninterrupted repose in his own Bhairava-consciousness; until the final moment, he carries out what has been taught through the vision of non-duality.
This alone is the vow of one who has cultivated the lotus-feet of a true guru; anything other than this is merely the withering away of the body. // 80 //
Summarizing what has been previously established, he declares the excellence of this teaching:

"Having realized that which is devoid of birth and destruction, known as the Supreme Lord (Paramārtha-Maheśvara), one remains at ease, having accomplished all that was to be done, due to the manifestation of the state of being the perceiver. (81)

Thus, in the manner just described, having realized the secret reality known as the Supreme Lord—which is the true Maheśvara—through firm conviction within one's own self and having experienced it correctly, he asks: "Of what nature is it? [The answer is: "It is devoid of birth and destruction," meaning that by attaining which neither birth nor death shall occur.
"He remains, having accomplished his purpose, as he wishes" means that having attained this, there being no further duty to be performed, he has achieved the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
As he desires, without transgressing his own will, he remains with his body sustained by his autonomy like the whirling of a potter’s wheel, passing his time.
How so? It says: "because of the manifestation of the state of being the perceiver.

Through the thorough cultivation of this secret, there is a manifestation—that is, a radiant vibration—as the experiencer in all states; therefore, even while situated in the body, he consists of full bliss. // 81 //
Thus, he states the absence of any restriction regarding the qualified practitioner:
"Whoever knows his own self in this way—as pervasive, as described, as the self of all, with diversity shaken off, and as incomparable supreme bliss—he becomes identical with that. (82)
In this manner—that is, by the method thus described—the all-pervasive Śiva, who is a single, undivided mass of consciousness and bliss, has been declared;

He has been made known through the process of cultivating reasoning, scripture, and direct experience. Whoever knows Him—any living being whatsoever who understands Him—becomes entirely free from limitation, becomes identical with Him, and is indeed Śiva Himself.

In this regard, there is no restriction regarding those qualified for the knowledge of one's own Self (*svātmajñāna*), because anyone at all—be they even animals tainted by the defects of birth, death, and so forth—becomes identical with that [Self] through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of their own Self as the Great Lord (*maheśvara*).
This is the reference of the word "whoever" (*ye kecana*). And of what nature is this Universal Self?

He whose self is the self of all subjects and objects of knowledge, or for whom all subjects and objects of knowledge are his self—he is, in other words, transcendent to all yet consisting of all. For this very reason, he has shaken off (vidhūta), that is, cast down, the infinity of diversity (nānātva) because of his constant and universal manifestation as the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa). Thus, being free from longing, he is incomparable (nirupama), devoid of qualifications, and possesses supreme bliss (prakṛṣṭa-ānanda)—such is he.
Knowing one's own self, everyone shall become of the nature of Śiva. // 82 //

Thus, having realized his own self as the Great Lord, he dispels such doubts as "Where shall he cast off his body when his authority over his own physical frame has expired? or "What state does he go to? [The verse states:

Whether in a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) or in the house of an outcaste (*śvapaca*), even if he casts off the body with his memory lost, he is liberated simultaneously with the dawn of knowledge; with his sorrow destroyed, he attains absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). (83)

Thus, having thoroughly cultivated his own true nature, the man of knowledge— whose heart is firmly consoled by the vision of supreme non-duality, seeing that all this is the sovereign freedom of the light of his own Self— whether casting off his body at a highly meritorious sacred site such as Prayāga, Puṣkara, or Kurukṣetra, or even in the abode of a dog-cooker, characterized as the home of an outcaste and most sinful, remains in either case free from the affliction of acceptance or rejection.

"Even so, through self-knowledge alone one attains isolation (*kaivalya*); that is to say, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains the state of absolute oneness (*kevalatā*), which is distinct from the entire range of causes and effects beginning with *pradhāna*, and which consists of a single mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*) in the form of that which transcends the fourth state (*turyātīta*).
This is because, for one who perceives this entire universe as filled by one's own Self, as being equal in vision, and as presided over by the Supreme Lord,"

For this very reason, the distinction between a sacred field (*kṣetra*) and a non-field is destroyed; likewise, the sorrow arising from the suspicion of dualistic thought is cast away by one who is thus [liberated]. As it has been said:
"Whether at Himavat, Gaṅgādvāra, Vārāṇasī, Kuru, or Prayāga, or in the house of a Caṇḍāla or the like, death is equal for those who know the reality of Śiva."
Thus, in the *Śrī-nirvāṇayogottara*, it is stated that mindfulness is not even required at the moment of the body's fall; this is expressed by the words "even one whose mindfulness is lost.
The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that let alone the case of having full recollection.

If, at the time of casting off the body, that knower— due to being overwhelmed by the wind, bile, and phlegm arising from it— loses his memory and, like wood or stone, becomes devoid of self-awareness, abandoning the physical frame helplessly, nevertheless, because he has previously attained knowledge of his own Self, he necessarily attains liberation (*kaivalya*); therefore, once the knowledge of one's own Self has been attained, there is no difference whether there is remembrance or non-remembrance at the time of death.

Now, let it be granted that for one who knows his own Self, there may be no distinction between a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) and a non-ford; however, as for the statement that "even at the time of death he might have lost his memory"—if, at the moment of the body's fall, he forgets that very knowledge of the Self which was previously adopted as the means, then how could he be liberated? As it has been said:
Even at the time of death, whoever departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, attains My state; there is no doubt about this.

Thus it is said in the Śrī Gītā. Even so, remembrance alone is the means here; for if one could attain the state of that [Lord] at the time of death even in the absence of remembrance of the Supreme Lord, then every common person, though deluded at the moment of death, would—due to the lack of distinction—attain union with the Supreme Lord.
To the objection that sentences such as these would therefore be invalid, he provides the answer: "He is liberated at the same time as [the arising of] knowledge.

It is true that there is no utility for him in memory; rather, at the very moment the true Guru imparts the instruction regarding the knowledge of one's own Self as the Great Lord into his ear, at that very instant, he ascends to the ultimate reality of the knowledge of his own Self—realizing "I am indeed all this"—and the state of being encased in the sheaths of Māyā and the rest dissolves.
He requires nothing else; he merely carries the body like the whirling of a potter’s wheel due to the persistence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Thus, there is no further torment for him regarding remembrance or non-remembrance in subsequent time. For it is only when there is a connection with the *kañcukas* of *āṇava* and *māyīya* born of ignorance that the bodily *kañcuka* arises. Through the instruction of the knowledge of one's own Self, the *kañcukas* born of ignorance perish; how then could the bodily *kañcuka* [persist]?

Since one who possesses knowledge is capable of imposing restraint [upon the senses] even when they are almost destroyed at the end, he would be liberated while still living at the very moment of explaining the knowledge of his own self.
As it is said in the *Sāhasrikā Kularatnamālikā*:
When the excellent guru explains it correctly, then without doubt, at that very moment he is liberated; he remains there like a mere machine.
Thus it is said; and in the venerable *Niśāṭana* as well:
"Whether for the duration of milking a cow, the flight of an arrow, or the blink of an eye, one who is joined even once to the supreme reality is liberated and shall liberate others."
Since he has previously, for even a moment, entrusted his self to Brahman by others,
how could there be any need for him to practice remembrance when the end of his life has arrived?

Thus it is said. Alternatively, by whom is the final moment of the knower of the Self experienced—experienced solely through his own self-awareness—by virtue of which its remembrance or non-remembrance might be postulated? Since that moment is not within the range of those with limited vision (*arvāgdṛś*), the omniscient ones (*sarvajña*) must be questioned regarding it; it cannot be determined from mere bodily movements at the time of death, even in the case of one who has realized the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It can be inferred as being either auspicious or inauspicious.

Therefore, for one who knows the knowledge of their own self and is constantly permeated by its state, the Supreme Lord—residing within that very self—surely causes them to remember His own true nature at the time of death, even if they have become like wood or stone.
As it has been said:
O Nārada, those mortals who, while engaged in their normal activities, remember me—
I remember them at the time of death as being like wood or stone.
Likewise,
when the mind is steady and the body is perfectly healthy, that man who remains established in the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmya) shall remember my universal form.
Then, when my devotee— who has become like a piece of wood or a stone— is dying, I remember him and lead him to the supreme goal.

Thus it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Lakṣmīsaṃhitā*. In this regard, the very fact of being constantly permeated by that state (*tadbhāva*) is the cause; otherwise, how could even memory occur at the end in the absence of the firmness of impressions (*saṃskāra*) from prior experience? Therefore, no one [can claim] that there is any utility for a knower (*jñānin*) at the moment of death. // 83 //

If, however, resorting to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like does not function as an auxiliary factor in any way whatsoever according to the manner described above, then why is it resorted to by the wise? To explain the distinction of the subject matter, he says:
"Service to sacred fords leads to merit; going to the house of a dog-cooker (an outcaste) at the time of death leads to hell.
But when there is no contact with the stains of merit or demerit, what is the use of that? (84)

For those wise ones whose grasp of the body and so forth as the subject (*pramātṛ*) has not yet dissolved, and who lack such confidence in the discussion of the knowledge of one's own Self (*svātmajñāna*), the performance of religious duties such as *iṣṭāpūrta* or even the accumulation of demerit, as well as the service of holy sites like Prayāga and the occupation of a sacred field (*kṣetra*) at the time of death, will certainly lead to merit and the attainment of the highest worlds.

"In the same way, there is the transition to death in the abode of a dog-cooker (śvapaca)" means that for these [beings], why would there not be a transition to death— that is, the attainment of demise— in an extremely wretched place characterized by the houses of dog-cookers and the like, leading to hell, such as the Avīci and other hells? This is because their grasping at the body as the subject of cognition (*pramātṛ*) still exists.

Having experienced even enjoyments according to their place of death, those who identify the body and so forth as the self would be of such a nature that they are born again in auspicious or inauspicious bodies and die again, thus forming an unceasing succession of birth and death. However, for one whose conceit of being an agent limited by the body and so forth has completely dissolved through the firmness of the reflective awareness of the knowledge of one's own Self— that person, whose nature is the sky of consciousness, experiences the cessation of contact with the latent impressions of the nature of merit and demerit.
Since that [conduct] has already occurred, what is the use of it?

Thus, because the adoption of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth belongs to those who partake in auspicious and inauspicious karma, such service to sacred fords and the like is of no use for the pure knower (*jñānin*). As it is said in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*:
King Yama Vaivasvata, who resides here within your heart—
if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to Gayā.

Thus: here, the conceit of identifying the body as the self residing in the heart is Yama; for those by whom that [conceit] has been consumed after they have realized the nature of the Great Lord who is their own full Self, how could there be for them this exertion of serving sacred bathing places and the like?
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta). // 84 //

Surely it was previously established that the Self—whose nature consists of the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* burned away by knowledge—remains established in its own true nature after the fall of the body and does not produce the sprout of rebirth, just as a burnt seed does not produce a shoot.

If the shattering of the bodily sheath occurs simultaneously with the manifestation of the knowledge of one's own Self, then let it be that there is no further rebirth; however, while the binding of the sheath of the body and so forth still exists, how could the Self not be permeated by the attributes inherent in it? Being thus permeated, would it not die?
How is it that one does not transmigrate? This objection is refuted by the example of rice grain from which the husk and chaff have been thoroughly separated;
once the rice grain has been cast out from within the husk and chaff, it no longer possesses identity with the nature of that husk. (85)
In the same way, when consciousness here has been separated from the veil of the sheaths through purification,
even while it persists, it becomes liberated and devoid of contact with them.
Just as when a grain of rice has been thoroughly separated and detached from its husk and awn,

the reinsertion of that husk and awn back into its original position— like the previous state— is such that, although the husk and awn remain capable of producing a sprout through their inherent nature, they do not achieve identity or firm integration with the grain; rather, the husk and the rice remain distinct, like two iron rods.

While remaining [in that state], they do not again become occupied with the production of a single effect; in the same way, for the knower, this consciousness—this sentience—is separated from the "sheath-cluster" (kañcukapaṭalī), the collection of sheaths such as the innate impurity (āṇavamala) and so forth. It is here extracted through the firmness of the cultivation of self-knowledge, [realizing]: "I alone am the nature of the Great Lord of my own Self, and I manifest everywhere at all times as the universal Self."

Thus, although she remains for some time within this veil of the bodily sheath (*kañcukapaṭalī*) in the form of a body through the persistence of residual impressions, she becomes one whose self is liberated, whose bonds are destroyed, and who is devoid of contact with that [sheath]. "Contact" refers to that coloring (*uparāga*) produced by the *kārma-mala*—consisting of merit and demerit—which arises from that veil of the body and so forth, and which is capable of generating the sprout of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). By that [contact], she is freed.
It becomes abandoned and avoided; for example, just as rice placed between husks is devoid of the capacity to sprout, so it is said:

first, cyclic existence has ignorance as its cause; however, for the yogin whose husk has been shattered by the arisen knowledge of one's own self, consciousness is no longer a cause for cyclic existence because the causal complex produced by ignorance is deficient, nor does it continue to persist for him.

This binding of the bodily sheath, though persisting by the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), has its root in ignorance burnt away by the fire of knowledge; thus, through the manifestation of its own inherent nature, it is no longer capable of producing the sprout of saṃsāra. Therefore, the knower, while still living, is of the nature of the Fourth (*turya*), and due to the absence of the body, is of the nature of that which transcends the Fourth (*turyātīta*); in either case, there is no further apprehension of saṃsāra. // 86 //

[Objection: "But surely, as long as it persists in the body through the remaining course [of karma], even the experience of the yogin who has realized his own true nature remains impure, because a degree of defilement caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body still exists. [Reply:
He refutes this with an illustration:
"The purity produced by a most skillful artisan [remains] due to the limiting adjunct of the casket..."
Even a soiled gem, when its adventitious impurity is removed, has a naturally clear ultimate nature. // 87 //
Thus, through the experience of the stainless state of the True Guru’s teaching,
even that which is liberated from the subtle adjunct appears as the form of Śiva, though it is devoid of any other adjunct.

Just as a gem, whose purity has been brought forth by a highly skilled lapidary, appears dirty or even greyish when it is enclosed within its setting, yet that very same gem, upon the removal of the condition of the setting and the absence of any further obstruction, becomes transparent in its ultimate nature and attains its true, stainless form exactly as it is.

In this very manner, this sensation belongs to one who stands in the stainless state of the teaching of a true guru, who possesses the science of the full knowledge of his own self, and who is the most excellent of instructors; it is such that its state is free from the impurity of *āṇava-mala*— which consists of time and serves as the foundation for the *māyīya* and *kārmika* impurities— through the constant cultivation of his teaching, which is the oral tradition (*mukhāmnāya*) concerning the secret of the knowledge of one's own self.

Through the destruction of the primordial impurity (*mala*), even that cognition which is of the nature of space—once liberated and separated from the "thin" adjunct (*tanūpādhi*), meaning the body as its defining characteristic or qualification—shines forth as the very form of Śiva. This means that after the dissolution of the body, it manifests as Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivatva*).

Just as a gem shines in its own true nature when freed from the adjunct of a casket, in the same way, consciousness—which is inherently pure through the realization of its own nature—becomes truly purified upon the destruction of the adjunct of the body, which was previously considered impure.
It shines.

Now, one might object: just as a gem, even when freed from the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its casket, becomes stained again by assuming another limiting condition, so too consciousness—though freed from the limiting condition of the body—if it were to grasp another limiting condition like the gem, then once again...
He refutes [the objection] that [it] is indeed impure because it possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), by stating: "even though it is devoid of other limiting adjuncts.

There is no absolute similarity between the example and the thing illustrated; for, upon the falling away of the body, all this which is considered a limiting adjunct shines as if it were one's own limb for that [Self] whose nature is the Great Light, the supreme non-dual form. Therefore, since there is no other limiting adjunct distinct from that, [it is not impure].
Furthermore, since that [Self] is qualified by another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is not comparable to the case of perceiving a gem through a limiting adjunct.

Indeed, the perception of the body as a limiting adjunct is rooted in ignorance; if that [ignorance] has been shattered by the axe of knowledge of one's own Self, how could there ever again be recourse to a limiting adjunct? As it is said:
"Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded."
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun.
Thus it is said in the Śrī Gītā.
Therefore, for the yogin, through the knowledge of his own true nature, self-awareness is always indeed pure. // 88 //
In the arising of all acquisitions (*upādhi*), the cause is solely the growth of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) through the practice of activities as they truly are; nothing new whatsoever arrives.
By means of unwavering faith based on the authority of the scriptures and so forth, one attains identification with that [very same state].
It is that very same person who previously attained heaven, hell, or human status. (89)

Whether through the authority of scripture, the oral tradition of the lineage of teachers, the cultivation of reasoning, or through faith rooted in prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a cognizer who has practiced either self-knowledge, or the rites of *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works), or the bound (*pāśava*) ritual action, attains at that very moment— through the growth of those impressions— a state of identity with them, that is, the essential nature of the respective object practiced; subsequently, upon the fall of the body, [he proceeds] in accordance with those impressions.

One attains heaven, which is unsurpassed joy; hell, which is the suffering of Avīci and other realms; or the human state, which consists of both pleasure and pain—that is, the human condition. It is not the case that something random simply falls upon a person at the mere falling away of the body, even if their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have not been cultivated. For every cognizer becomes of whatever nature they habitually cultivate with a particular intention; however, this occurs at the time of death.

The sense is that whatever object is desired with clarity attains manifestation for the knower; thus, there can never be a reversal regarding a familiar object, nor can anything unfamiliar ever appear as something entirely new. Therefore, in all cases, prior habituation alone is the cause. // 89 //

Thus, for one who knows their own Self, the state of being constantly permeated by that [realization] is the cause for the full manifestation [of reality] at the moment of leaving the body; it is not, however, some visible worldly occasion of death consisting of merit or demerit that serves as the cause for heaven, hell, and so forth. Rather, the final moment, while nourishing a virtuous or sinful condition within that [process], becomes an auxiliary factor for the deluded; but once liberation has been attained, it is no longer a cause. (90)

Even those animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth, who know their own state of existence as being that very self, go to that destination, for they have been refined by the impressions of ancient awakening.

When the knower has been established in this way, the final moment— the last instant coinciding with the destruction of the body— whether it nourishes and partakes in a state that is meritorious or sinful as inferred by nearby perceivers on account of the imbalance of the bodily elements or the experience of a malignant disease,
becomes the auxiliary cause or the instrumental factor for those deluded perceivers who identify the body with the self.

Let the wretched one go; yet, by this much alone, he cannot become the cause—the instrumental reason—for that yogin’s departure from the body and the attainment of another body, provided that yogin has not had his bodily self-conceit shattered and remains ever skilled in the contemplation of his own Self as the Great Lord (Maheśvara). To demonstrate how this [conclusion] follows, he says: "Even those who... and so forth.

Even those who, due to some underlying intention or by means of a curse and the like, have attained birth in a sinful womb or even the form of an animal, should recognize their own state— their own abiding nature— at the time of death as being the Self; though they are deluded, they attain that state of the Self, sustained by the awakening of the latent impressions of self-knowledge previously cultivated.

In the case of the liberation of Gajendra and similar instances, when even an elephant—though possessing the nature of a beast—had the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of devotion to the Supreme Lord awakened through prior practice, he praised the Blessed Viṣṇu and, having completely cast off his outer casing, attained his own true nature (*svarūpa*). What was the cause for that recollection? The underlying point is this: a knower (*jñānin*), though acting like a piece of wood or a stone due to the influence of the humors (*dhātu-doṣa*) arising from the body and so forth, [remains unaffected by] merit, sin, or even a cat stepping over him.

Or, when one abandons the body while uttering some kind of incoherent speech, there is no loss whatsoever of the knowledge and other qualities practiced during one's time of sound mental composure; for the attributes residing in the body and so forth fall away with the body itself, but they cannot obstruct that which has been constantly cultivated. Thus, until the very moment of death, thorough cultivation alone is the ultimate reality in all circumstances.
As it is said in the Gītā:
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state."
Likewise,
to those who are constantly devoted and who worship Me with love,
I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
Thus, it is precisely the cultivation of the internal organ that is the cause for attaining the ultimate state. // 91 //

Thus, for one who has seen this view, since the state of being constantly permeated by that [previous] existence is cast aside as something new, nothing unprecedented occurs at the destruction of the body; for the wise person, it is the body alone that is perishable—it is only that which perishes, and not the sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Demonstrating this, he says:
Consisting of heaven and consisting of hell, this person situated within the interval of the body attains union with another body upon its destruction, according to his own fitness.
Thus, at the moment of realization, in whatever manner one's own self appears to him once and for all, it remains exactly so even after the fall of the body; it does not become otherwise.

Therefore, the person (puruṣa) residing within the body, the jar, and so forth—the self (ātman) of everyone, permeated by the impurity of karma (kārmamala)—is one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is perfumed by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the fruits of actions performed with the intention of attaining heaven and the like; thus, being characterized by the fully developed latent impressions for the fruit of heaven, he is "consisting of heaven" (svargamaya), meaning he is the enjoyer of the fruit of heaven.

Likewise, when the latent impressions of previous evil deeds have fully developed, he is the enjoyer of the fruit of hell. The body alone is the locus for the enjoyment of the fruits of both types of karma.

"Upon its dissolution, according to one's own fitness" means that when that body perishes, the self (*ātman*), in accordance with its own deposited latent impressions (*vāsanā*), immediately enters into a connection with another locus of experience— a different body— and subsequently becomes a partaker of the enjoyment of the fruits bestowed by specific karmic impressions.
In the same way, at the occasion of knowledge— that is, at the time when the teacher reveals the nature of the Self to the disciple— the Self is consciousness (*caitanya*).

Just as it once appeared—once, that is, a single time—in accordance with the sequence of instruction, having reached a state of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by either limited or perfect freedom, in that very same way does it always manifest for the Knower. By whatever nature his own Self has been reflected upon at all times, by that very form it unfolds due to the growth of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); it is not merely manifested [in this way] upon the fall of the body.
Even so, the self of the knower is otherwise veiled;
for that which has appeared cannot be unappeared, otherwise no one would practice anything at all, and there would be a total collapse of all worldly activity.
By dharma there is upward movement, and by adharma there is downward movement.
Liberation results from knowledge, while bondage is held to result from its opposite.

All such [doctrines] would thus be rendered inconsistent; therefore, at the time of death, let the body be as it may—rather, the sprouting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing within one's own self is the sole cause for everyone’s bondage and liberation.

If, however, due to an imbalance of the elements (dhātu), the agony of death is experienced within the body, this does not cause any impairment to the growth of one's practice; rather, it merely brings about the state already described: the derangement of the collection of sense organs, the loss of memory, the distressing irregularity of breath, and the severance [of functions].
There are specific pains in the vital points (marmans), which constitute the experience born from the refinement of the body. // 94 //
How could he not remain so even when engaged in conflict? Thus, even when engaged in delusion, at the time of death, the Knower does not fall away from the ultimate reality of his own self. (95)
The complete deprivation—that is, the loss of its own essential nature—of the group of thirteen instruments, both external and internal, is as follows:

the sense organs, such as the eyes, are no longer capable of perceiving objects such as forms; likewise, the organs of action, such as speech, do not engage in speaking, grasping, and so forth; nor does the intellect determine an object according to reality; and there is instability of the mind and egoism.
Even so, they remain in the midst of existence as formative impressions (*saṃskāra*).

Likewise, there is the loss of memory, which is the forgetting of an experienced object; even when entreated by kinsmen, one on the verge of death does not recognize an object standing before them, though it has been experienced hundreds of times. For this very reason, there is a constant cultivation of that state.

At the time of death, without the discourse on the knowledge of Brahman or other such teachings, no other gift or anything else takes root in the mind—like a painting in the sky—but rather there is the injunction that one must simply perform the prescribed duties (*itikartavyatā*).
Likewise, "breathing" refers to the air in the throat; its "confusion" is a hoarseness or a hiccup in the region of the throat.
Furthermore, there is the cutting of vital points (*marman*), the tearing of bone-joints, as well as specific types of pain such as fever, diarrhea, and so forth. Thus,
that which arises from the bodily refinement due to the imbalance of the elements of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣma*) within the body, which is like a sheath for the [true] being;

Experience (*bhoga*) is the perception of suffering born of the body; how could that not occur, and by what means could it be avoided, when there is conjunction with a physical form? It would certainly occur even for a knower (*jñānin*). For that reason, the knower—who has always rendered the conceit of the body and so forth into a state of subjection, and who is permeated by the nature of the Great Lord as his own Self—remains rooted in the true essence of the reflective awareness of consciousness, which is the supreme reality of the Self, even during the connection with bodily ignorance produced at the moment of death.
He does not fall away nor undergo transformation;
for that knower, having cast off the connection with the body, cannot be made identical with it by the experience born thereof.

He merely does not perceive [the world] for a moment immediately after the falling of the body, as is the common saying of the world—this being all that pertains to him whose heart is established in its own nature.
For one who has practiced devotion to the Lord with a mind established in its own natural activity according to its own intended purpose, nothing unprecedented occurs;

therefore, it has been demonstrated hundreds of times previously that the knower is liberated immediately upon the manifestation of his own Self, and the residual impressions of the body do not bestow bondage upon him.

But how can one who always identifies the body as the self and consists of merit and demerit not come to be absorbed in that [body], which is produced by the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth arising from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the body? As it has been said:
"When the embodied being meets its dissolution while goodness (*sattva*) is predominant, then he attains the stainless worlds of those who know the Supreme."

And so forth. Qualities such as *sattva* and the rest are attributes of *prakṛti*; they exercise their constraint only upon one who is composed of them. However, for one who has cultivated [the self] as being distinct from them, these qualities are nothing at all; thus, the path of the Knower (*jñānin*) is entirely different.
On the other hand, those limited subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*) who have not beheld the feet of the Guru project their own internal attributes onto another.

For instance, by what means can those who dispute on many grounds— claiming, "If this person were truly a knower (jñānin), why does he eat and dress when his body is afflicted by disease and the like? or "Why has he fallen into a state of stupor at the time of death, thinking 'I remember nothing'?"— be refuted, since they themselves are obscured by ignorance (avidyā)?
If this knower were possessed of bodily attributes and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), what harm would come to him by that?

For the knower, the light of his own Self (*svātmaprakāśa*), though variegated by various states, remains the light of his own Self alone; there is no destruction of it as the experiencer of its own Self, whereby knowledge would perish.

Even the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, whose greatness consists of the fullness of the six divine qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*), experienced pain from being struck by the hunter’s arrow during his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, [while remaining within] a physical body.

Having considered that he "renounced" [the body], one might ask: did the Lord of the Universe suffer any loss of his own essential nature? From a worm up to Sadāśiva, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the body is exactly the same; however, the distinction is this much: one has a body accompanied solely by the reflective awareness of one's own Self (*svātmapratyavamarśa*), while the other possesses a false reality consisting of the conceit of identity with the body and so forth. Therefore, the physical attributes of the knower and the ignorant are indeed similar, yet there is no equality of fruit on this account—this very point was stated in the *Gītā*.
Even a man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature;
all beings follow their nature—what can restraint accomplish?
Thus [ends verse] 95.

Now, demonstrating that the cause for the cultivation of the yoga of knowledge—whether by the non-sequential or the sequential method—is indeed the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*) in its various forms, he describes the difference in results:

"When one immediately attains this path of ultimate reality from the mouth of the Guru, then, due to an extremely intense descent of power (*atitīvraśaktipāta*), one becomes Śiva without any obstacle. (96)

At the very moment when a person in their final birth, having heard from the mouth of a Guru— that is, from the mouth of an eminent teacher— this path of ultimate reality which has been explained in hundreds of ways, namely the secret path of the oral tradition consisting of the awakening to one's own self characterized by perfect sovereignty,
approaches and enters it, at that very time, at that very instant, immediately following the Guru’s instruction, he becomes free from obstacles.
Having performed [this], one becomes Śiva himself;
as it is said in the *Śrīkula*:
"Whether with ease, or even in play, or else with reverence, the knower of reality [attains this]."
O beloved, he upon whose eyes one casts one's gaze is liberated at that very moment.
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might ask: "How can such a secret oral tradition (*mukhāmnāya*) be imparted? To this he replies: "By the descent of the most intense power" (*atitīvraśaktipātāt*).

This refers to the descent (*pāta*)—the arrival within the heart-lotus of the bound soul (*paśu*)—of that supreme Lord's power known as grace (*anugraha*), which is exceedingly intense and piercing; by means of which even a bound soul becomes Śiva through the knowledge of the guru’s oral tradition, meaning he is liberated while still living.

Just as the substance of copper becomes gold through the application of an alchemical elixir (*siddharasa*), so too the attainment of self-knowledge occurs solely through the means of the Supreme Lord’s grace. In this matter, the power of destiny (*niyatiśakti*) does not apply as a means—such as recitation, meditation, sacrifice, and the like. However, for one whose heart has been pierced by the power of grace, the secret oral tradition from the mouth of the deity forcibly and instantaneously captivates the heart.
Because by means of this one attains the state of the Supreme Goddess instantaneously, the descent of power (śaktipāta) from the Supreme Lord is manifold and beyond questioning. // 96 //

Furthermore, for one upon whom the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred through the gradations of medium, weak, or very weak, and who contemplates through the sequence of yoga until the moment of death according to the teacher’s instruction, there is the attainment of Śiva-nature at the fall of the body; for him who ascends by way of the steps of the ladder, there is the state of being identical with Śiva at the final limit upon the attainment of ascent into the Supreme Reality. // 97 //

Thus, it is said that for one who, due to the dullness of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), fails to obtain the instruction of complete knowledge, yet resorts to and directly realizes the form transcending all [levels], whose essential nature extends to the limit of all the *tattvas*—how does this occur? He says:

"by the sequence of the steps of the ladder. The "steps" are the forms of the *kanda*, navel, heart, throat, *lambikā*, *bindu*, *nāda*, and *śakti*; they are indeed the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) for ascending upwards.

The "attainment of their station" refers to the process of gradual withdrawal and ascent—progressing slowly from the *kanda* to the navel and then to the heart—and the yogi's entry [into those states] by means of that process.

Thus, until the realization of the sprout of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) at the moment of the "falling of the body," the yogi comes to abide in the nature of Śiva through this sequence; this is the logic of the sequential method that has been explained. // 97 //
