Even so, for a yogi practicing the sequential method who has attained composure, such ascension may not occur and an obstacle may arise to the attainment of the desired goal; therefore, he dispels the doubt as to what would happen if death were to occur before the ultimate reality has been realized, by stating: "But for him who has not reached the stream consisting of the supreme reality, there is a resting in the middle."
Even for one whose mind is eager to attain that state, death may nevertheless occur at any time. // 98 //
One who has fallen from yoga is described in the scripture as a lord of worlds of variegated enjoyment;
by virtue of reaching a state of rest, he becomes Śiva in another birth. // 99 //

Thus, for one who practices yoga by means of this method of skipping [levels], if—due to some obstacle—he comes to rest midway and, having obtained an experience in some *cakrādhāra*, becomes satisfied with that very place; consequently, failing to reach the stream consisting of the ultimate reality (*paramārthamayī dhārā*), which is the state promised as the nature of the supreme principle (*paratattva*) and transcending all paths (*sarvādhvottīrṇā*); or even if his mind remains eager to attain that state—

Even for one who has made a vow and desires to establish the existence of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sattā*), if a misfortune should occur midway, then what will be the fate of this person who has failed to obtain what was to be obtained from the alms-gathering? To this he says: "one fallen from yoga," and so forth.
Such a person is said—that is, declared—in the *śāstra*, the scriptural treatise, to have fallen away or deviated from yoga, that is, from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), in both ways.

To the question "Of what kind would he be?", he says "Variegated" (*citra*) and so forth. Merely by the falling of the *piṇḍa*, he becomes the Lord (*pati*) or Sovereign (*īśvara*) over those worlds which consist primarily of variegated enjoyments— namely, various wonders such as women, food, drink, garlands, garments, ointments, song, and instrumental music— which are conducive to his own repose and are locations belonging to the Lords of the Principles (*tattveśvara*).
The meaning is that immediately after death, he is endowed with divine enjoyments.
Then, when his authority over those enjoyments has been exhausted, how could that one who has fallen from yoga exist again? To this, he says "viśrānti" and so forth.
By virtue of the location of the place of rest, such as the *kanda* and so on, through the power of awakening the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that practice, he—

Having been born in a second life—that is, in another birth—and having obtained in the cycle of existence a qualified body fit for the practice of yoga, he resumes with effort the yoga previously practiced; then, effortlessly ascending to the state consisting of the supreme reality as promised in his former birth, he becomes Śiva himself upon the falling away of the physical body. // 99 //

Now, for the yogi who, despite practicing yoga, fails to find even the slightest rest in any single point due to mental instability, yet remains possessed of faith toward yoga—what will his destination be after the fall of his body? To this he says:

"Indeed, having practiced this path of ultimate reality but not having attained yoga itself, one partakes in the enjoyments of the celestial realms and rejoices with a joyful mind for a very long time. (100)
Just as a sovereign emperor is honored by all people within his realm,
so too is one who has fallen from yoga honored at all times by all the gods throughout the worlds.

Even if one has practiced this path— the true nature of self-knowledge— which has been explained hundreds of times, and has served it with faith and devotion, yet fails to attain the rest characterized by yoga as it truly is due to the instability of mental defects even during the course of a single life, and should he die then, that "fallen from yoga" (yogabhraṣṭa) [is saved] by the power of the grace resulting from the faith and devotion firmly rooted in the subject of the yoga of knowledge.
Sharing in the enjoyments of the divine realms and with a joyful heart, he experiences delight for a very long time; he becomes worthy of worship by the gods themselves in their respective worlds.
To the question "Who is like him?", the author says "The All-Knowing One," and so forth.

Just as a sovereign king, a universal monarch who rules over the seven continents, is honored and worshipped by all people throughout various regions and territories, even so is this one— who has exhausted the domain of both merit and demerit, in whom dispassion has arisen,
and who is in his final birth— to be revered by us, for he was the one who exerted himself in a previous life for the sake of inquiry into the Self.
That is to say, he is praised even by the gods. // 100 // 101 //
He states what occurs immediately after his cessation of the authority over enjoyments in other worlds:
"Having regained human status after a long period of time and having practiced yoga, he attains divine immortality, from which he does not return again. (102)

Having enjoyed pleasures in the celestial worlds as previously described for a very long time, that one fallen from yoga returns to the human state in this cycle of existence; having obtained a body fit for the practice and means of yoga, he effortlessly attains that very same yoga which was difficult to reach in his previous birth due to mental restlessness, because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of yogic tendencies— rooted in devotion and faith born in the past— have been awakened in his mind.

Having attained and practiced this, at the end of the body one realizes the divine nectar which is the nature of the supreme reality; that is to say, one attains firmness in the state of the supreme self-nature.

For this very reason, there shall be no returning for him from that state. Thus, even a slight reflection upon this great auspicious object, which is the knowledge of one's own Self, does not lead to the path of saṃsāra.
As it is said in the Śrī Gītā:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear."
Thus: "Likewise,
one who lacks perseverance, though endowed with faith, whose mind has wavered from yoga, not having attained perfection in yoga..."
Beginning with such questions as these, [it is said:
"One who has attained perfection through many births then goes to the supreme goal."
Thus, even though the entire treatise ending with this final section has been expounded by the Sage, it must be remembered. // 102 //

Thus, for a living being who has been touched even slightly by this sequence of the yoga of knowledge, there arises such a preeminent degree of majesty that it cannot be described; therefore, he demonstrates that those whose hearts are moistened by discernment (*viveka*) should, with their whole being, be vigilant toward the cessation of birth and death: "Therefore, whoever is devoted to this true path attains the state of Śiva."
Thinking thus, one should strive for the ultimate reality in whatever way possible. // 103 //

Since the practice of self-reflection (*svātmapratyavamarśa*) thus leads to the attainment of the supreme fruit through the sequence of stages already explained, it is therefore shown that there is no restriction regarding the qualified practitioner (*adhikārī*)— that anyone at all may be devoted to this most auspicious path, the way that brings about the highest liberation. Any person whatsoever, tormented by hundreds of afflictions such as birth, death, and disease, who is "devoted" (*nirata*) with a discerning intellect (*vivekabuddhi*) to the very end...
Devoted to that very [path] and becoming full of faith, that living being, having immersed himself therein, attains the state of Śiva in no long time;
having shaken off all the afflictions of worldly existence, he reaches the condition which is the supreme good in a single birth alone.
As it is said in the scripture *Śivadharmottara*:
Let this liberation in a single lifetime first be examined;
by whom is liberation over many lifetimes denied for you?
Thus; having reflected in this way and considering it so, one must strive—that is, exert oneself with great effort—in that ultimate reality, by whatever means possible.

Since effort directed toward the primary goal is fruitful, one should not allow even the slightest negligence regarding this matter. For if, through the practice of yoga, a firm rooting of the Self within oneself arises, our desired aim is accomplished;
if not, at least the attainment of another divine world is secured.
Even for one who has returned from that state, through the power of awakening the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of yoga previously practiced, there is once again a connection with yoga;

thus, by cultivating the path to the highest good, nothing adverse befalls the practitioner. Therefore, one should not harbor even the slightest pride regarding the means of attaining the supreme human goal. May there be auspiciousness! 103.

Thus, having established the instruction on the *Paramārthasāra* as taught by the venerable Śeṣa, supported by reasoning, experience, and scripture according to the sequence of the non-dual teaching of Śiva, the author of this treatise— seeking only his own satisfaction and preceded by the disclosure of his own name—
declares the conclusion of the work’s meaning, defining that this very instruction is the means for accomplishing the supreme human goal (*parapuruṣārtha*).
For one who meditates upon this supreme Brahman as summarized by Abhinavagupta, the state of Śiva—the penetration of one's own heart—attains him very soon indeed. (104)
This has been set forth at length to establish that for a person who meditates upon the Supreme Brahman— the most excellent, which, by virtue of its expansive nature, consists of perfect bliss,
and which is one's own essential self— there occurs, without effort and through mere reflection upon one's own self, a realization of it very soon, rather than only at the end of many births.

Thus, for one who has become such a Brahman, the state of Śiva is attained and the realization of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) becomes possible. How so? By effecting an entry into one's own heart—that is, by entering one's own heart, which is the locus of reflective awareness (parāmarśa). Of what nature is that Brahman? It is of such a nature wherein the essence (saṃkṣepa), meaning the intended purport (tātparya), has been proclaimed and revealed by Abhinavagupta through his celebrated name.

And here, under the guise of a name, this too may be said: that which is "new" (*abhinava*)—the supreme secret of the *parabrahman* not seen by others—and which was "hidden" (*gupta*), as if concealed; such a thing has thus "arisen" (*udita*), meaning it has been revealed. That *brahman* is of such a nature.
By communicating this, the rarity of the instruction would be established. (104)
Describing the extent of the work, the author states his authorship in this treatise:
"This very essence of the scriptures, which is exceedingly profound, has been condensed by me, Abhinavagupta, illuminated by the remembrance of the feet of Śiva, in one hundred Āryā verses. (105)

This essence of the treatises—the most excellent reality among many books—has been condensed by me; for that which cannot be established even by thousands of volumes has here been accepted and stated in a brief measure of one hundred verses. By this, his skill of genius is expressed:
"By whom? By me, who am illumined by the remembrance of Śiva’s feet."

Śiva, whose nature is supreme bliss, who abides in his own self, and whose singular form is consciousness and bliss—his "feet" are the rays of consciousness. To "remember" them means to perceive them at the very moment of grasping objects such as sound, and to never lose the experience of them in every instant.
Illumined by this, one becomes radiant with the wonder of supreme I-consciousness; for this reason, his name is to be celebrated.

Otherwise, how could one who identifies the body and so forth as the self, and whose true nature as the Great Lord (Maheśvara) remains unknown, be qualified as an author for such an extensive teaching of the Great Purpose? For it is said that "one who possesses a certain nature is capable of discerning that very nature";
thus, by this statement, the teacher is declared to possess the nature of the Great Lord who has entered [into him]. May there be auspiciousness! 105.
Thus ends the *Paramārthasāra*, composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara Ācārya Abhinavagupta.
By me, the disciple of that Śrīmat Kṣemarāja—who possessed the oral tradition of the true gurus and had directly realized Maheśvara—[this work is composed]. // 1 //
This commentary, named *Yoga*, which consists of the full non-duality, has been composed by the ascetic Virakta, whose abode is the city of Śrī Vitastā. // 2 //
This *Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti* is complete; it is the work of the venerable and supreme devotee of Maheśvara, the illustrious Rājānaka Yogarāja.
